en: The Net-Shredding Commentary on the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, Fascicle One, composed by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu of Lingfeng.
The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is transmitted from mind to mind; when Bodhisattvas compose treatises to elucidate the sutras, it is likewise nothing other than this.
Because it is a single great matter, it is said:
"Seeking thoroughly throughout the ten directions."
There is no other vehicle whatsoever;
even if one were to skillfully guide the various capacities of sentient beings through gradual and gentle instruction.
From the perspective of the power of implementation,
various paths are taught,
just as there are three types of grass and two types of trees.
Although the moisture received differs,
the rain that moistens it originally consists of but a single flavor.
Therefore it is said:
"It is like eating rock honey;
it is sweet both in the center and at the edges."
It is further said:
"Both coarse words and subtle speech all return to the primary meaning."
How could one possibly seal off the text and lose its essential meaning,
perversely clinging to names and marks to dissect the void?
Furthermore, as for the World-Honored One Maitreya,
his traces abide in the position of the successor;
his fundamental nature must necessarily be inconceivable.
Asaṅga and Vasubandhu were both the assistants who supported [the Buddha] at the Dragon Flower Assembly.
In that case, how would they differ from Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra?
As for Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna, both were included among those granted prophecies by the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha].
As transmitters of the Buddha’s mind-seal,
their writings must certainly not be mutually contradictory.
Thereupon, later generations of lecturers would arbitrarily and falsely judge, saying:
"Vasubandhu [authored] the *Viṃśatikā*."
This is the Initial Teaching of Establishing Characteristics;
Nāgārjuna’s *Madhyamaka-śāstra* is the Initial Teaching of Destroying Characteristics.
Aśvaghoṣa’s *Awakening of Faith* belongs to the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) while also incorporating the Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao); neither, however,
is the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Alas! How profoundly they have failed to reflect.
For Vasubandhu established the doctrine of Consciousness-Only based upon the Yogācāra school.
First, one uses the doctrine of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra) to refute the dual grasping at self and phenomena.
Next, it is clarified that consciousness itself is like an illusion and is not truly existent.
Therefore, it is also called the "Treatise Destroying Form and Mind.
Is it appropriate now to designate it as the "Teaching that Establishes Characteristics"?
Nāgārjuna, relying upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā,
thoroughly dispelled the self-clinging of the four natures to reveal the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Therefore, it is said:
Those who wish to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas should study Prajñāpāramitā.
It is also said:
If this emptiness did not exist,
nothing whatsoever could be accomplished; it is because the principle of emptiness exists that [all things are possible].
Everything can indeed be accomplished.
Is it then appropriate to designate this now as the "Teaching that Destroys Characteristics" (Poxiangjiao)?
Aśvaghoṣa, by means of the gate of the True Suchness of the One Mind,
reveals the profound Prajñā taught according to wisdom; and by means of the gate of the Arising and Ceasing of the One Mind, [he reveals the conventional teaching].
This reveals that the eight consciousnesses of the Yogācāra are taught according to conventional understanding;
thusness is precisely the one true dharma-realm.
It is that which unifies phenomena and principle while simultaneously transcending them.
Arising and ceasing are precisely the phenomena constituted by the totality of principle.
This is the principle that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
Since the two gates are not separate from the one mind,
there is not a single instance of arising and ceasing that is not the totality of True Suchness.
There is not a single instance of True Suchness (tathatā) that does not fully possess arising and ceasing;
this is precisely the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (shishi wuai fajie).
To now claim that it differs from the Consciousness-Only (vijñaptimātra) or the Middle Way (madhyamaka) treatises is incorrect.
Nevertheless, it is not yet the perfectly consummate One Vehicle; is this not so?
Moreover, within the sūtras and śāstras...
It is further asserted that True Suchness and all phenomena are neither identical nor different, just as water and its waves are.
The evidence for this is fully present;
how can one permit such partiality and dogmatic adherence? For if one were to say that [the nature] is definitively one, [it would contradict the facts].
If suchness is neither arising nor ceasing,
then all phenomena must also be neither arising nor ceasing;
otherwise, all phenomena would be subject to arising and ceasing.
It would certainly be untenable for True Suchness (tathatā) to likewise undergo arising and ceasing. If, on the other hand,
one says they are definitively different...
In that case, True Suchness would not be the actual nature of all phenomena;
it would instead exist outside of all phenomena,
having a separate location and direction.
To claim that it is neither permanent nor all-pervasive is particularly untenable; therefore,
the *Awakening of Faith* states that True Suchness (Tathatā) undergoes perfuming.
For example, when one touches a wave,
one is touching water; thus,
the attachment to the notion of distinctness is refuted.
From the beginning, it has never been stated that True Suchness (tathatā) undergoes transformation through the influence of perfuming (vāsanā).
As for the claim that Consciousness-Only (vijñaptimātra) holds True Suchness to be unperfumable,
it is like the analogy of waves when water is stirred.
The nature of moisture is non-static;
thus, it refutes the attachment to a fixed, singular [reality].
From the very beginning, it was never stated that there exists a separate, immutable *tathatā* (suchness). As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* says:
Unlike other schools,
which maintain that apart from form, mind, and so forth, there exists a real and eternal dharma called *tathatā* (suchness).
Furthermore, it says:
"True Suchness is precisely the real nature of Consciousness-Only.
The clear evidence is as manifest as this.
Later generations have thus slandered Yogācāra by misrepresenting it as "stagnant True Suchness" (tathatā);
how great is their transgression!
That being so, what the Yogācāra calls "true" means that the [subjective] aspect and the [objective] characteristic are non-distinct.
This is precisely the "Gate of Suchness" within the single mind of the *Awakening of Faith*;
it corresponds to what is called the "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, wherein phenomena appear as distinct.
This is precisely the "Gate of Arising and Ceasing" within the single mind of the *Awakening of Faith*.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra states:
"The various consciousnesses have three kinds of characteristics, namely: the characteristic of transformation."
Regarding the "characteristic of karma" and the "true characteristic," the *Zongjing* commentary explains as follows:
The arising of the mind is called "transformation" (pariṇāma), because it arises simultaneously with the eight [consciousnesses]; thus,
all possess both arising and ceasing.
Therefore, it is called the characteristic of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*). Movement constitutes karma;
all eight consciousnesses are mobile.
All that is called the characteristic of karma;
the true nature of these eight is all called the true characteristic.
Viewed from this perspective,
it is clear that both the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* take the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* as their primary authority.
Since the fundamental tenets are identical,
then all names and meanings naturally do not contradict one another.
Consequently, commentators were unable to establish names based on their meanings; instead,
they arbitrarily established meanings based on names,
resulting in the two treatises being as discordant as water and fire.
How lamentable! This *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* exists in two versions within the canon.
The first was translated by Paramārtha of the Liang dynasty;
the second was translated by Śikṣānanda of the Tang dynasty.
These two translations have been compared and collated.
The Tang edition is even more elegant in its phrasing and more consistent in its meaning;
however, as the Liang edition has already been widely circulated,
I did not dare to act solely on my own judgment.
He respectfully decided by drawing lots before the Buddha;
having drawn the one that favored the "Exegesis of the Tang Edition," he was finally able to exhaustively clarify even a slight glimmer of understanding within a fleeting moment.
Having completely dissected the deluded attachments of both schools, it is titled *The Commentary on Tearing the Net*.
It was written with the brush on the eighteenth day of the tenth month of the Gui-si year; thus the preface is recorded.
This is explained in two parts:
first, the explanation of the title;
second, the explanation of the text.

First: The Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra, composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of the Tang Dynasty. Regarding the five characters of the title, there are four distinct points.
One communication.
To speak briefly: there are three levels of subject and object.
"Awakening Faith in the Mahāyāna" (Dacheng qixin) means "arousing faith in the Mahāyāna";
this is the specific title.
The single character "treatise" (lùn) constitutes the general title.
As for the mention of "three layers" (triple weight):
First: the treatise is that which gives rise [to faith],
and Mahāyāna faith is that which is given rise to.
Second: faith is that which is capable of believing,
and the Mahāyāna is that which is believed in.
Third: "Great" (mahā-) serves as the qualifier,
and "vehicle" (yāna) is that which is qualified.
This is explained in three parts:
first, an explanation of the Mahāyāna;
second, an explanation of the *Awakening of Faith*.
Third, the explanation of the words of the treatise.
First, the explanation of "Mahāyāna" is divided into two parts;
first, the analytical explanation.
Next is the combined explanation.
This, in turn, is divided into two parts.
First is the explanation of "Great" (mahā).
Next, the vehicle (*yāna*) is explained.
First, regarding the explanation of "Great" (*mahā*): it is absolute, transcending all dependencies and having nothing external to it.
It is provisionally named "Great" because it directly points to the present, infinitesimal nature and mind of sentient beings,
which by its very nature is endowed with the three meanings of the Greatness of Essence, the Greatness of Attribute, and the Greatness of Function.
This refers precisely to this present, momentary mind,
which remains unchanging while following conditions,
its entire substance being true suchness (tathatā).
This is called the Greatness of Essence.
Within this very essence, in which all delusion is itself true,
there are inherently present merits numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges that accord with the nature of reality.
It does not decrease among ordinary beings,
nor does it increase among sages;
this is called the greatness of its characteristics.
This very essence and characteristic of the mind-nature remains unchanging while following conditions,
giving rise to the causes and effects of the ten realms, both defiled and pure.
Upon realizing that this dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature,
one is able to transform defilement into purity;
this is termed the "Great Function."
Regarding the essence:
apart from the essence itself, there are no separate characteristics or functions,
just as there are no waves of water apart from its moisture.
Therefore, the essence is beyond dependence.
When speaking of characteristics,
there is no essence or function existing separately outside of those characteristics.
Just as there is no moisture apart from water and no waves apart from it,
their characteristics are mutually dependent; thus, they are spoken of in terms of function.
Thus, function has no separate essence or characteristic apart from it,
just as there is no moisture or water apart from waves; therefore,
function is beyond all conceptual relativity.
These three great elements are neither identical nor different;
they are inconceivable.
It is solely this one mind;
therefore, it is called "Great.
Next, I shall explain the term "vehicle" (*yāna*).
It is named after its metaphorical function;
its essential meaning is that of "carrying across.
This refers directly to the present, infinitesimal nature and mind of sentient beings.
By the very nature of phenomena, it carries one to the stage of Buddhahood,
for its benefit of self and others proceeds without cessation.
This is what is called a "vehicle" (yāna).
The essence of the nature of mind is great;
this is the vehicle of principle (li-yāna).
Pervading from antiquity to the present,
it is eternally unchanging; thus,
the nature and characteristics of the mind are great.
This is precisely following the vehicle (yāna),
because it is never separate from or detached from it,
remaining in constant association.
The function of the mind-nature is great;
this is precisely the attainment of the vehicle,
like the seven treasures of a wheel-turning monarch.
Because of the accomplishment of mastery,
the three greatnesses are inherently complete;
this is collectively termed the Vehicle of Principle (Lī-yāna).
Because there are no three distinct entities,
the illumination of the nature constitutes cultivation;
at the time of cultivation, there are the three greats.
Collectively, these are called "conforming to the vehicle" (yānānuvartin), because they accord with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and realize the fruit from its cause.
At the stage of fruition,
the three greatnesses are collectively termed "attaining the vehicle," because of their ultimate sovereignty.
Nature and cultivation are non-dual;
cause and effect are non-dual.
Therefore, this present, momentary mind-nature is designated as the vehicle.
The first part of the explanation is concluded.
Next, regarding the combined explanation:
although the nature of the mind of sentient beings is, in the present moment, merely infinitesimal, it is [the source of all].
This is precisely the inconceivable Mahāyāna; yet,
through the causes and conditions of delusion and awakening, and the perfuming of defilement and purity,
there subsequently arise the distinctions of the ten dharma-realms.
That is to say, if one becomes deluded regarding this single mind and gives rise to the ten evil deeds of views and afflictions,
it will carry sentient beings into the three evil realms;
this is called a "crippled donkey and a ruined carriage."
If one knows to fear the sufferings of the three miserable realms,
one should practice the ten wholesome paths of action as well as the various meditative concentrations of the form and formless realms.
Thus, they transport sentient beings to the three wholesome realms;
furthermore, being fearful of the suffering of the triple world,
they cultivate the supramundane studies of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Having eternally escaped the wheel of suffering,
they then transport sentient beings and lead them into the city of Nirvana.
It is called the sheep-cart.
If one knows that the twelve links of dependent origination are fundamentally without intrinsic nature, [one attains this vehicle].
Realizing that its essence is fundamentally empty,
one brings the wheel of delusion, karma, and suffering to eternal rest;
thus, one also carries sentient beings across to enter the city of nirvana.
Although lacking great compassion,
they still serve as a supreme field of merit for sentient beings;
this is called the "deer cart."
If one contemplates that both self and others are together within the wheel of suffering,
and aspires to deliver them all,
one is fully endowed with great compassion.
They give rise to great vows,
universally able to transport and carry sentient beings,
gradually leading them toward the city of unsurpassed, great nirvāṇa.
This is called the "ox-cart.
If one thoroughly realizes this present, momentary nature of the mind,
it is itself the inconceivable Mahāyāna.
By deeply contemplating that the moving mind is itself neither arising nor ceasing,
one immediately attains entry into the gate of True Suchness (tathatā),
beginning from its very designation.
When it reaches the stage of contemplative practice,
continuing until the ultimate stage,
one's own effort in cultivation is completed.
It continuously carries others without ceasing;
this is called the Great White Ox Cart,
which is now referred to as the Mahāyāna.
This specifically refers to the great white ox-cart,
as it distinguishes [the true vehicle] from the three carts outside the gate.
Furthermore, all sentient beings...
Although this nature of mind is deluded such that its entire substance becomes a ruined donkey-cart and the three carts and so forth,
nevertheless, this nature of mind...
Remaining unchanging amidst changing conditions,
it has never failed to be the ultimate Mahāyāna; it is,
for example, like pure gold.
Even though it may be fashioned into various types of impure vessels or miscellaneous utensils,
the nature of the gold remains unchanged.
It remains as precious as before.
If one knows that the defiled vessel is in essence pure gold,
then one may utilize the pure gold found within that defiled vessel.
Therefore, its light shines upon Avīci;
it is not difficult to suddenly leap over the ten stages;
one need only lay down the butcher’s blade.
Thus, one becomes counted among the thousand Buddhas.
The parrot attained śarīra relics through mindfulness of the Buddha;
the white dove turned its rebirth toward the ancestral path upon hearing the sutras.
Therefore, it is pointed directly that the deluded and illusory nature of the mind of all sentient beings is itself the Mahāyāna.
Previously, the Great was used to distinguish from the Small;
this was explained in terms of relative opposition.
This is precisely the meaning of the "gate of arising and ceasing.
The latter refers to the small becoming the great;
this is explained from the perspective of absolute transcendence.
This is precisely the meaning of the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Within the momentary, fleeting mind present before all sentient beings,
these two gates are inherently and naturally possessed.
Because they are inseparable,
it is called the Mahāyāna. This concludes the initial explanation of the Mahāyāna.
The two explanations of the *Awakening of Faith* are also twofold:
first, an analytical explanation;
second, a synthetic explanation.
The detailed explanation is further divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of arising;
second, the explanation of faith.
First, regarding the explanation of "arising":
Question:
Among all dharmas...
There is no birth and no arising.
Why, then, do you speak of arising? Answer:
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) neither arises nor does it not arise.
If one were to speak only of arising...
In that case, one loses the meaning of the Gate of True Suchness (shēn rú mén).
If one speaks only of non-arising,
one loses the meaning of the Gate of Arising and Ceasing (shēng miè mén).
If one says that it both arises and does not arise,
these are mutually contradictory.
If one says that it neither arises nor does not arise, [it is likewise untenable].
This immediately becomes conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
One should know that all four positions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are inexpressible;
provided one does not fall into emotional attachment.
In accordance with the four *siddhāntas*,
because there are causes and conditions,
it may also be spoken of.
What is now called "arising" is actually neither arising nor non-arising; it is spoken of as arising only by way of discourse. Why is this so?
The single mind is absolute and beyond dependence;
fundamentally, there is no distinction between that which can believe and that which is believed.
Yet, one is deluded regarding this single mind.
Then immeasurable doubts arise,
like water turning into ice;
this is the inversion of delusion.
Thereupon, perfect and eternal right faith arose,
like ice returning to water; though delusion and awakening are distinct, they are fundamentally one.
Because the single nature is immovable, it does not arise;
its nature neither increases nor decreases.
Delusion and enlightenment are distinct;
therefore, it is not that they do not arise. Thus, arising is itself non-arising.
It arises without arising;
it is with reference to this that "arising" is discussed.
The wondrousness lies therein.
Indeed, although faith arises with great fervor,
it remains but a single mind;
there is no distinction between the one who believes and that which is believed.
There is neither subject nor object;
yet there is subject and object.
Both subject and object are, in their very essence, the single mind-dharmadhātu.
Just as a lamp has illumination that,
in turn, illuminates the lamp itself;
therefore it is said:
To give rise to faith within one's own mind and,
in turn, have faith in one's own mind—
this is the unsurpassed Dharma-gate of the Arising of Nature.
Next, regarding the explanation of faith (*śraddhā*):
according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, among all the virtuous mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*), [faith is defined as follows].
It is the foremost of all [virtuous mental states],
characterized by a pure mind that consists of profound patience toward, and a longing for, reality, virtue, and capability.
It counteracts lack of faith;
its function is to delight in the good.
The commentary says:
However, regarding the distinctions of faith,
there are briefly three types:
first, faith in actual existence.
That is to say, because one possesses profound faith and acceptance regarding the reality and principles of all phenomena;
second, because one has faith in their excellence.
This means that because one has deep faith and delight in the true and pure virtues of the two jewels,
one possesses the third [type of] faith: the conviction in their capacity.
That is to say, one has deep faith that all mundane and supramundane virtues have the power to bring about the attainment of pleasant results.
It can accomplish the noble path because it gives rise to aspiration; by means of this,
it serves as the antidote to that mind of lack of faith.
One delights in realizing and practicing mundane and supramundane virtues.
As stated in the present treatise:
"Faith is of four kinds."
First is faith in the root,
which means delighting in mindfulness of the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness).
Second is faith that the Buddha is endowed with boundless virtues.
This means that one constantly delights in paying homage, making offerings,
hearing the Dharma, and practicing it,
in order to dedicate these merits toward all-knowledge.
Third, faith in the Dharma brings great benefit,
because it leads one to constantly delight in practicing the various pāramitās.
Fourth, faith in the Saṅgha of Right Practice.
This refers to constantly making offerings to the assembly of bodhisattvas,
because they correctly cultivate practices for their own benefit and the benefit of others.
One should understand from the *Prajñapti-śāstra* that [the dharmas] truly exist.
This is identical to the present treatise’s first [point], which holds that faith is the root;
and to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*’s second and third [points], which hold that faith consists in recognizing excellence and recognizing capability.
This corresponds to the second, third, and fourth types of faith discussed in the present treatise.
Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
"This is the mental factor of faith (*śraddhā*)."
Its intrinsic nature is limpid and clear,
and it is also able to purify other minds and mental factors,
like a water-clearing jewel.
It can clarify turbid water.
Furthermore, all defiled phenomena each have their own distinct characteristics.
Only lack of faith is turbid by its own nature;
furthermore, it is able to turbid other minds and mental factors.
Just as extremely filthy things defile themselves and others,
faith is the exact opposite of that.
Therefore, purity is its characteristic.
This is because the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha remains immutable while conforming to conditions.
The entire body constitutes all mind-kings and mental factors;
yet these all mind-kings and mental factors remain unchanging according to conditions,
each and every one being without exception the totality of the Tathāgatagarbha-nature.
Therefore, although this single term "faith" is analyzed according to conventional truth,
it is nothing more than one among the various virtuous mental factors (citta-saṃprayukta-dharma).
In reality, this is the entire substance of the *tathāgatagarbha*,
not merely a partial aspect of it; furthermore, although all defiled mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*) exist, [they do not constitute its essence].
All of these are likewise the entire substance of the storehouse nature (ālaya-vijñāna); however,
because they run contrary to this nature,
many faults and transgressions arise.
It is like a vessel made of gold that has been defiled;
it is unfit for handling or enjoyment.
Only this faith [is worthy].
Because it accords with the nature [of reality],
it possesses manifold merits;
it is like a crown made of gold for a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).
This makes their dignity even more manifest;
therefore, once faith is established,
all wholesome dharmas [follow].
There is nothing that does not correspond with them.
The initial section-by-section explanation is concluded.
Next is the combined explanation.
Now, although the dharma-gate of the arising of nature is indeed inconceivable,
it consists of the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing.
Thus, it is not uniform;
some may believe in heterodox and inverted views,
giving rise to delusion and creating karma.
In this regard, one is said to have no faith in the True Dharma,
or perhaps to have faith in the causes and effects of the mundane world.
Thus, the ten wholesome actions of humans and devas, as well as the meditative absorptions of the form and formless realms,
are termed "outflow-tainted wholesome" (*sāsrava-kuśala*).
Alternatively, it refers to the arising of faith in the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
This constitutes the supramundane dharma-gates of the two vehicles,
termed untainted virtue (*anāsrava-kuśala*).

Alternatively, one may give rise to faith in the fruits of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) and unsurpassed *nirvāṇa* through the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgraha-vastūni*).
This constitutes the Bodhisattva’s dharma-gate of self-benefit and benefit for others,
termed the goodness of the Middle Way; or,
it is the arising of faith in the inconceivable, non-contingent Mahāyāna within the present, infinitesimal nature of the mind.
This constitutes the unsurpassed, perfect, and sudden Dharma-gate,
termed the "Excellence of the One Vehicle.
Now, one should precisely give rise to this inconceivable faith in the One Vehicle.
Therefore, it is said that "Arousing Faith" continues the lineage of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, while the teachings frequently speak of faith, understanding, practice, and realization (*śraddhā-adhimukti-caryā-sākṣātkriyā*),
here we speak only of "arousing faith."
It does not speak of the arising of understanding, practice,
or realization; faith is the dharma-realm,
and all dharmas tend toward faith.
Because there is no separate practice or realization apart from faith;
that is to say, although all sentient beings may lack faith in the sublime principle of the Mahāyāna within their own minds.
Though they give rise to delusions and create karma,
the nature of their faith has never diminished in the slightest.
It is like water turning into ice;
its moist nature remains unchanged.
This is called "the principle as such" (li-ji) giving rise to faith.
If one hears this treatise and is able to know that the present, infinitesimal nature of the mind is itself the Mahāyāna.
This is called giving rise to faith through names and designations.
If one can contemplate this nature of mind in every thought-moment,
one will know that such thought is itself non-thought.
Not giving rise to ignorance or various delusive inversions—
this is called the arising of faith in contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
If one spontaneously eliminates coarse defilements, [this is the result].
Purifying the six sense faculties is called giving rise to a semblance of faith;
if one enters the stage of correctness, it is called true faith.
From the Stage of the Pure Mind up to the Ultimate Stage of the Bodhisattva—
this is called the stage of partial realization of faith.
If one transcends the bodhisattva stages,
subtle conceptual discrimination is ultimately and forever exhausted.
The fundamental nature of the mind is eternally present;
this is called giving rise to ultimate faith.
Therefore, it is simply called "Arousing Faith.
This concludes the second explanation of "Arousing Faith.
Third is the explanation of the "Treatise" (śāstra).
It refers to that which, through debate, investigation, and analysis, makes incisive judgments and provides clear exposition,
thereby enabling one to attain certainty.
If one relies upon language and written words to reveal the ultimate meaning and counteract false attachments.
To discern the characteristics of practicing the right path and to exhort others to cultivate it is the certainty of the teaching.
One is able to give rise to a semblance of faith through the contemplative practices of hearing, reflection,
and cultivation. If one examines and investigates the five aggregates,
such as form, and all phenomena:
All are unaccomplished;
knowing that the deluded, moving mind is itself neither arising nor ceasing.
This practice is definitive;
it can give rise to the faith that partially realizes the Ground of Pure Mind and the like.
If one enters the gateway of suchness, [this occurs].
Permanently severing both associated and dissociated defilements,
one suddenly uproots the root of ignorance with a single moment of associated wisdom.
This principle is definitive;
it can give rise to ultimate faith in all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Therefore, it is called the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna).
This treatise was composed by the Great Master Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, the twelfth patriarch of the Western Heaven, during the sixth century after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
it is the comprehensive compendium of both the nature (svabhāva) and characteristics (lakṣaṇa) schools.
The words are concise while the meaning is vast;
it is truly the definitive Mahāyāna,

Both the expressive and the expressed are termed the ten directions of the Dharma;

The one of infinite mastery of wisdom has perfected the four types of gnosis of enlightenment,

2. Second is the greatness of mind,
which refers to the four great vows.
Third is the greatness of understanding.
This refers to the perfect and constant faith-understanding (adhimukti).
The four purities are the stage of the pure mind-ground (śuddhābhūmi).
Purifying the two types of conceptual discrimination;
the five adornments of greatness,
namely merit and wisdom.
Sixth is greatness of time,
referring to three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Seventh is greatness of completeness.
That is to say, unsurpassed bodhi.
The preceding six are the causes of the Mahāyāna.
The latter one is the fruit of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding "possessing the Dharma":
The Liang edition reads "dharma" (法).
This corresponds to what is called the "subject" (*dharmī*) in the context of *hetuvidyā* (logic),
which serves as the basis for the thesis (*pakṣa*).
This refers to phenomena produced through causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*),

As for "phenomena" (*dharma*):
The Liang edition reads "meaning" (yi).
This refers to the principle or truth (satya) revealed [by the teaching], analogous to what is called the "predicate as the essence" (uttara-pakṣa-svabhāva) in the science of logic (hetuvidyā).
This is to clarify the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
Second, the explanation has two parts.
First, the explanation of the existence of phenomena.
Second, the explanation of the phenomena (*dharma*).
Now, for the first:
regarding the statement "there are phenomena":
This refers to the mind of all sentient beings;
this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Based on this, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed: it universally examines that which is produced through causes and conditions.
All are dharmas that exist;
all are precisely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
All can manifest the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
Therefore it is said:
"Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—
these three are without distinction."
However, for a beginner, if one were to have them contemplate the Buddha-dharma,
the doubt would be that it is too lofty.
If one were to instruct them to contemplate the dharmas of sentient beings,
the scope of doubt would be too vast;
therefore, one only instructs them to contemplate the mind.
Furthermore, fearing that people might erroneously claim there is a separate true mind apart from the minds of sentient beings,
[the text] establishes only the minds of all sentient beings as the object of contemplation.
Now, to mention the Buddha-dharma is to encompass all mental phenomena and the phenomena of sentient beings;
to mention the phenomena of sentient beings...
This encompasses all Buddha-dharmas as well as mental dharmas.
Now, by taking up even a momentary mental dharma of a living being manifest before us,
one encompasses all the dharmas of sentient beings as well as the Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore, it is said that this encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Based on this infinitesimal mental dharma manifesting before sentient beings,
the meaning of Mahāyāna is revealed.
This is a single manifestation;
it is a manifestation of all things, manifesting each and every phenomenon of sentient beings and each and every Buddha-dharma as it is raised.
There is nothing that is not the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
Thus, the Lotus Sūtra says:
"The great chariot made of the seven treasures."
Their number is immeasurable.
Because this characteristic of the suchness of mind (*cittatathatā*) reveals the essence of the Mahāyāna, it is precisely this momentary, arising mind that is present before us.
It is not within, not without, and not in between.
The past has no beginning;
the future has no end;
the present has no limit.
It is not characterized by existence; it is not characterized by non-existence;
nor is it characterized by both existence and non-existence.
It is neither the characteristic of non-existence nor the characteristic of existence;
it is neither the characteristic of birth-and-death nor the characteristic of nirvana.
It is not the characteristic of the two extremes;
it is not the characteristic of the middle way;
it is not a characteristic that can be expressed in words.
It is not the characteristic of being inexpressible;
it is not the characteristic of being both expressible and inexpressible;
it is not the characteristic of being neither expressible nor inexpressible.
Because there is no other alternative,
it is forcibly designated as the "characteristic of true thusness" (tathatā-lakṣaṇa); this very [characteristic] is true thusness itself.
This is the essence of the Mahāyāna;
there is no other separate essence. One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
The mind of sentient beings is an existent phenomenon;
this is the essence and tenet of the Mahāyāna.
The reason is as follows:
Because it is the characteristic of true thusness (*tathatā*).
It is analogous to the direction upon which delusion and awakening depend;
yet the direction itself is neither delusion nor awakening.
This is the characteristic of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of this mind.
Because it can manifest the essence, characteristics, and function of the Mahāyāna, this very true suchness (tathatā), which is the unchanging substance of the mind,
manifests arising and ceasing as its entire substance follows conditions.
That is to say, according to the conditions of defilement and purity,
one fully creates the ten dharma-realms; although one creates these ten realms, [the nature remains unchanging].
The ten realms are all provisional designations devoid of intrinsic nature;
they remain unchanging amidst conditions,
and their very substance is the ultimate truth.
Thus, it is able to reveal the essence of the Mahāyāna.
Due to following defiled conditions,
ignorance falsely arises.
There is that which is seen and that which is not seen; it appears impure,
and is neither permanent nor blissful.
It is not self, not pure,
and not tranquil;
it is subject to change.
Lacking self-mastery,
it was endowed with false and defiled states exceeding the sands of the Ganges;
now, by overturning these defilements, they are transformed into purity.
Ignorance does not arise;
there is no seeing and nothing seen;
the nature of the mind is unmoving.
There is no other dharma to be further sought;
it is precisely within suchness that the meaning of the great light of wisdom is established.
The meaning of universally illuminating the dharma-realm;
the meaning of truly and perfectly knowing;
the meaning of being pure by nature.
The meanings of permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
the meanings of tranquility, immutability, and sovereignty;
and the meanings of the fulfillment of pure merits exceeding those of the sands of the Ganges.
Thus, they are able to manifest the characteristics of the Mahāyāna.
Because they dwell together with sentient beings within the ocean of saṃsāra,
they are finally willing to take pity on themselves and pity others.
They give rise to great vows,
cultivate great merit and wisdom,
and realize the fundamental Dharma-body.
Spontaneously giving rise to inconceivable activities,
they bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future.
Thus, it is able to manifest the function of the Mahāyāna. Consequently,
the very essence of the present, momentary mind is itself the essence of the Mahāyāna.
The appearance of delusive phenomena within the present mind is itself the characteristic of the Mahāyāna;
it is the functional activity within the present mind.
This is precisely the function of the Mahāyāna;
yet, due to the causes and conditions of sentient beings' delusion and defilement,
they do not realize it in their daily lives.

It is by virtue of the existence of the causes and conditions of delusion and defilement that the causes and conditions of awakening and purity are established; it is by virtue of the existence of the causes and conditions of awakening and purity [that they are so designated].
This clearly reveals the greatness of essence, characteristic,
and function; therefore, it is said that "this mind's characteristic of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions can manifest the essence, characteristic, and function of the Mahāyāna."
For example, when water freezes into ice,
its moist essence and its function of moistening are both no longer visible.
If one knows that the ice field is water,
one employs skillful means to cause it to melt;
only then can the moist essence, the characteristic of fusion, and the function of lubrication be manifested.
If one does not contemplate the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the mind,
then one cannot manifest its essence, attributes, and function;
it would be like clinging to solid ice.
There is nothing to be utilized.
Even if one were to set aside the mind directed toward sentient beings and seek the Mahāyāna elsewhere, [it would be of no avail].
Nor can it manifest the greatness of its essence, attributes, and function;
it is like when, during a great freeze,
one discards the solid ice.
There is no other water.
May those who study the Mahāyāna reflect upon this deeply.
One should formulate the syllogism as follows:
The mind of sentient beings is the subject (dharmin);
it can manifest the essence, characteristics, and function of the Mahāyāna—this is the thesis (pakṣa).
The reason given is:
"Because it is characterized by the causal conditions of arising and ceasing.
The common analogy is: "It is like becoming disoriented because of one's reliance on spatial directions."
Because of delusion, one awakens to the directions.
First, the explanation of the "possessor of the dharma" is complete.
Second, the explanation of the "two dharmas."
First, the explanation of the general meaning;
second, the explanation of the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*).
Now, the first.
That which is called "Dharma" briefly consists of three kinds: first,
the greatness of essence (svabhāva-mahattva).
This refers to the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena;
whether in a state of defilement or purity,
its nature is eternally equal.
It is without increase and without decrease,
because it is without differentiation. What was previously called "the characteristic of suchness of this mind" indicates the essence of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the statement that "all phenomena are suchness":
because the suchness of the mind is itself the suchness of all phenomena.
This is because of the non-dual suchness.
All phenomena consist of both defiled phenomena and pure phenomena.
Briefly stated, there are the five categories and one hundred dharmas;
extensively stated, there are the ten realms and the thousand suchnesses.
Take whichever single dharma you may grasp.
This is the entire substance of True Suchness (tathatā) and not merely a partial aspect; therefore,
it is said that its nature is eternally equal.
At the time of awakening, there is nothing gained;
at the time of delusion, there is nothing lost.
Furthermore, the *tathatā* within a mustard seed or the tip of a hair is not small.
The suchness of the precious realm of Mount Sumeru is not great; therefore,
it is said to be without increase and without decrease,
a single characteristic that is without characteristics.
They are inseparable;
therefore, it is said that there is no distinction. Now, since it is stated that "all phenomena" (sarvadharma), [it follows that...]
Furthermore, the statement that [the nature] exists within defilement and within purity refers entirely to the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing; yet,
it is said in accordance with this that its nature is eternally equal.
Because there is neither increase nor decrease and no differentiation,
one knows that the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing are themselves the gate of True Suchness (Tathatā).
Therefore, the subsequent passage states that they are "mutually inseparable.
If one were to abandon the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing,
by what means could one realize and embody True Suchness (Tathatā)?
If one clings to the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing,
by what means could one possibly comprehend True Suchness?
Second is the magnitude of its characteristics.
This refers to the Tathāgatagarbha,
because it is primordially endowed with immeasurable and boundless inherent qualities. This means that the very momentary thought manifesting in sentient beings is itself the Tathāgatagarbha.
Now, True Suchness (tathatā) remains unchanging while conforming to conditions;
its entire substance manifests as the infinitesimal mind of sentient beings.
Thus, this infinitesimal mind—
This is the entire substance of True Suchness (tathatā).
That it is now also called the Tathāgatagarbha is in reference to the gate of arising and ceasing.
It is called the "Tathāgatagarbha" when hidden and the "Dharmakāya" when manifest; thus,
the Dharmakāya and the Tathāgatagarbha [are one].
Although there are two names,
ultimately there is no duality of essence;
therefore, it is not merely when manifesting as the Dharmakāya that the name is revealed.
It is endowed with the characteristics of immeasurable and boundless intrinsic qualities;
that is to say, even while it is currently designated by the name "Tathāgatagarbha," it has from the very beginning been fully endowed with immeasurable and boundless intrinsic qualities.
Third is the greatness of function (*mahā-vṛtti*):

because it can give rise to all causes and fruits, both mundane and supramundane. Indeed, within this very momentary mind of sentient beings as it manifests before us, there is no dharma that is not fully present.
There is no dharma that is not created;
that is to say, according to the conditions of defilement or purity,
one fully creates the ten dharma-realms.
It is universally capable of producing the causes and effects of the ten realms; however,
when speaking specifically in terms of the nine realms,
this includes the causes and effects of all evils such as the three miserable destinies.
Although these are also functions of this very mind,
they are like using gold to fashion a filthy vessel,
or using a sharp sword to cut mud.
To use a supreme jewel as a pellet for a slingshot cannot be called a great application;
it is merely the cause and effect of the outflows belonging to humans and devas.
Although this too is a function of this mind,
it is not called a "great function" if one uses a mani jewel merely to trade for a single garment or a single meal.
Although the uncontaminated cause and effect of the two vehicles are also functions of this mind,
they are like empty space holding Jāmbūnada gold.
If it does not produce profit or interest,
it cannot be called "Great Utility.
This refers to the causes and effects of the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of Bodhisattvas of the provisional vehicle.
Although it possesses the function of benefiting both oneself and others,
it is like using Jambūnada gold for commercial trade;
it has not yet attained sovereign mastery over all things.
Nor is it called the "Great Function.
Although one may aspire to the ultimate fruit,
it is like crafting a royal jeweled crown out of Jāmbūnada gold.
Being unable to uproot their dwellings and ascend to the heavens,
they are not yet said to employ the Great [Vehicle].
They possess only the spiritual lineage of the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna-gotra*).
Know that this present, momentary mind is in essence identical to True Suchness (tathatā),
endowed with boundless virtues.
One is then able to observe that all delusive thoughts are signless;
out of compassion for oneself and others,
one gives rise to great vows and practices in accordance with the nature of reality.
Extinguishing beginningless ignorance,
one realizes the fundamental Dharmakāya and spontaneously gives rise to inconceivable activity.
The various distinctions of sovereign activities pervade the entire dharma-realm,
being equal to true suchness (tathatā).
For example, if one refines Jambūnada gold into an elixir of immortality,
one can then uproot one's entire residence and ascend to the heavens.
Because they sport with mastery,
it is called the Greatness of Function.
Question:
The function within the fruit is vast;
it manifests forms throughout the nine realms and occasionally appears within the three miserable paths.
One should also produce the causes and effects of evil;
why then do you speak only of the causes and effects of good? Answer:
In order to deliver sentient beings,
he manifests the causes of evil;
yet fundamentally, there is no delusion or defilement.
This is untainted goodness;
for the sake of delivering sentient beings,
he manifests the experience of evil retribution.
Nor is there any painful sensation;
it is like the bliss of the third dhyāna.
Therefore, it is designated simply as a wholesome cause and effect.
Furthermore, that which is said to be able to produce all causes and effects of goodness refers to its great function within the fruit:
it universally acts as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for sentient beings.
This means causing the arising of all mundane and supramundane wholesome causes and effects;
it does not mean that once one has already attained Buddhahood,
one personally generates mundane and supramundane wholesome causes and effects.
All the various manifestations of the Buddhas are the profound functioning of the mastery of *tathatā* (suchness),
and all accord with the pure and wondrous virtues of *nirvāṇa*.
Because it cannot be called a real cause and effect.
Question: Since the application of the "Great" (Mahāyāna) is based on the fruit of Buddhahood, [how can it be so?]
What is meant by the "characteristic of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of this mind"?
Answer: If there were no sentient beings' minds, [there would be no such characteristic].
Then there would be no essence or characteristic of the Mahāyāna;
if there were no essence or characteristic of the Mahāyāna,
where could there be the function of the Mahāyāna?
Question:
Since it is said that this is the "profound function of True Suchness" (tathatā),
why is it not attributed to True Suchness itself?
This then pertains to the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing.
Answer: If it were not the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing, [it would not be so].
If even the name "True Suchness" (Tathatā) does not yet stand,
how can one distinguish its great function?
Now, the mind of sentient beings that arises and ceases in the present, even for a mere instant—
its essence is True Suchness (tathatā),
and its phenomenal aspect is the Tathāgatagarbha.
Functioning thus, it is able to give rise to all causes and effects,
yet people use it daily without knowing it;
this is called the "principle-as-such" (li-ji) Mahāyāna.
If one can know that this single mind has a great essence, a great characteristic, and a great function,
this is called the "name-as-such" Mahāyāna.
If one can observe that deluded thoughts are without characteristics...
This is called the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) which is itself the Mahāyāna.
If the coarse defilements fall away first,
the six sense faculties become pure.
This is called the "semblance" Mahāyāna;
this treatise names it "semblance awakening.
If one can personally realize its essence, characteristics, and functions, [one attains true awakening].
Progressing spontaneously,
this is called partial realization, which is itself the Mahāyāna.
This treatise designates it as "partial awakening" (anupūrva-bodhi).
If the fundamental nature of the ultimate mind abides eternally and manifests before one,
this is called the ultimate, which is the Mahāyāna;
this treatise designates it as "Ultimate Enlightenment."
Sixth, it is eternally immediate;
from beginning to end, it is equal.
This is precisely the True Suchness Gate of this mind.
The immediate and the constant are each sixfold;
their rising and sinking differ greatly.
This is precisely the gate of arising and ceasing of the mind.
Therefore, the minds of all sentient beings are established as existing phenomena to reveal the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
This concludes the initial explanation of the meaning of "Great" (Mahā).
Second, the explanation of the meaning of "vehicle" (yāna):

because it is that which all Buddhas have fundamentally ridden upon, and because all Bodhisattvas ride upon this to enter the stage of Buddhahood. This further refers to the person who rides [the vehicle].
In order to manifest the Dharma that is mounted upon,
it is said: "That which is called the Mahāyāna."
This is the vehicle upon which all great beings, such as Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, ride. Indeed,
there are no sentient beings whose minds do not fully embody the three greatnesses (mahā) of essence, attribute, and function.
These three great elements are themselves called the vehicle (yāna),
and for the sentient beings of the nine realms, [they serve as such].
One cannot exhaust the utility of this Great Vehicle mind;
it would be a waste to instead create the inferior vehicles of the donkey, sheep, deer, or water buffalo.
Only all Buddhas [can do so].
Having already mounted this Great Vehicle,
they have reached the ultimate stage;
such is the case for all bodhisattvas.
All ride upon this Mahāyāna and thereby enter the stage of Buddhahood; therefore,
one must necessarily rely on the minds of sentient beings to manifest the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
The second section, "Establishing the Meaning," is completed.

Composed by the Lingfeng śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu. Part Three: The Section on Exegesis.
This is divided into two parts: first, the structural outline; second, the actual exegesis. Now, the first:
what is the Section on Exegesis?
This is of three kinds:
namely, for the purpose of revealing the true meaning,
and for the purpose of counteracting false attachments.
By discerning the characteristics of practicing the True Path, one reveals the ultimate meaning to eliminate doubt and counteracts false attachments to remove clinging;
this is precisely what gives rise to faith.
To discern and practice the characteristics of the true path is precisely what constitutes the succession of the Buddha-lineage. Second,
the correct understanding has three parts.
First, the revelation of the true meaning;
second, the counteracting of erroneous attachments;
third, the differentiation of the characteristics of practicing the right path.
This consists of three parts:
first, a general presentation of the two gates;
second, the individual explanation of the two gates.
The three fetters are shown to be inseparable;
this is the first [point].
Herein, that which reveals the true meaning is as follows:
Based on the one mind,
there are two gates:
namely, the gate of the suchness of mind.
This is the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind.
These two gates each encompass all phenomena.
Because they are thus successively inseparable, "one mind" refers to the infinitesimal momentary mind manifesting before sentient beings.
As for the phrase "two gates":
It is not that front, back, left, and right constitute duality;
rather, it is simply the unchanging amidst following conditions.
Thus, this very mind of arising and ceasing is called the gate of True Suchness (tathatā).
"Unchanging yet following conditions":
this very Tathatā-mind is called the gate of arising and ceasing.
This is precisely what is meant by the saying that "this house has but a single door."
This is also what is called "the single path to nirvana for the Bhagavans of the ten directions.
Yet, when one is deluded regarding it, birth and death begin;
thus, the entire substance of True Suchness (Tathatā) becomes subject to arising and ceasing.
To awaken to this is for saṃsāra to cease;
thus, birth and extinction are, in their very essence, true suchness (tathatā).
Therefore, two gates are elucidated based on delusion and awakening.
Furthermore, to speak of awakening in contrast to delusion is the gate of birth and death;
yet, delusion and awakening are equal.
This is the gate of true thusness (*tathatā*).
To say that these two gates each encompass all phenomena means that,
with respect to the gate of true thusness:
Thus, the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, as well as the five positions and hundred dharmas, are all subsumed therein;
each and every one is none other than True Suchness (tathatā),
whose nature is eternally equal.
There is neither increase nor decrease,
because there is no differentiation; this is stated with reference to the gate of arising and ceasing.
It also encompasses the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, as well as the five stages and hundred dharmas;
not a single one among them is without arising and ceasing,
including all the dharmas of the six classes of ordinary beings.
These are accomplished through the causes and conditions of delusion and defilement;
the various dharmas of the four noble ones are accomplished through the causes and conditions of awakening and purity.
In both the mundane and supramundane realms,
there is not a single phenomenon that is not manifested through the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing;
thus it is said that these are mutually inseparable in their successive progression.
This means that apart from the *tathatā* (suchness) of the single mind,
neither arising nor ceasing can be found;
it is like being apart from spatial directions.
There is no delusion or enlightenment apart from this;
it is just as there is no ice or water apart from the nature of moisture.
Apart from the arising and ceasing of the one mind,
there is likewise no such thing as true thusness (tathatā) to be found;
it is like being apart from delusion and awakening.
There is no other method;
it is just as there is no separate nature of moisture apart from ice and water.
Question:
For what reason are two gates demonstrated based upon a single mind?
Answer: All phenomena (dharmas) naturally possess these two gateways.
Therefore, when the Buddhas preach the Dharma,
they always rely upon the two truths:
the gate of the suchness of mind.
This is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
The gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Although they are called the two truths,
they are in fact but a single reality;
therefore, the two truths are perfectly interfused.
They are inconceivable;
therefore, each encompasses all dharmas,
and they are mutually inseparable.
Furthermore, when the entire nature gives rise to both the two cultivations of the contrary and the compliant,
it is called the gate of birth-and-death;
yet the entirety of these two cultivations— contrary and compliant— does not alter the single nature.
It is called the gate of True Suchness (tathatā-mukha).
Furthermore, when the entire principle manifests as phenomena,
it is called the gate of arising and ceasing (utpāda-nirodha-mukha).
The totality of phenomena is itself the principle;
this is called the gate of True Suchness (Tathatā).
Furthermore, one may distinguish between phenomena and principle.

That which is called the gate of arising and ceasing involves the manifestation of phenomena and principle; that which is called the gate of true thusness is the total cessation of both phenomena and principle.
Furthermore, that which is provisional yet real is called the gate of True Suchness (tathatā);
that which is real yet provisional is [the gate of phenomena].
It is called the gate of arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, by distinguishing between the provisional and the real,
it is called the gate of arising and ceasing.
The non-duality of the provisional and the real is called the gate of True Suchness (Tathatā).
Furthermore, it is for the sake of the real that the provisional is established.
Based on the gate of true thusness (tathatā), the gate of arising and ceasing is explained;
the provisional is opened to reveal the real,
pointing out that the gate of arising and ceasing is itself the gate of true thusness.
Furthermore, the manifestation of the provisional for the sake of the real, and the revelation of the real by opening the provisional,
both belong to the gate of arising and ceasing.
In principle, it is neither provisional nor ultimate;
it is named the gate of True Suchness (tathatā).
Furthermore, it is explained according to wisdom.
Thus, arising and ceasing are themselves the gate of True Suchness (tathatā);
according to conventional sentiment,
True Suchness is itself the gate of arising and ceasing.
Explaining according to the capacities of sentient beings and their wisdom,
there are two gates based upon the single mind.
Question:
Since these two gates are themselves the two truths,
what then are the seven kinds of two truths?
How are they mutually inclusive?
Answer: If that which truly exists is conventional, [it is so].
Ultimate existence as cessation is the truth;
the conventional is subsumed within the gate of arising and ceasing as that which is associated with grasping.
The ultimate is spoken of in conjunction with it.
This is subsumed under "semblance-awakening" within the gate of arising and ceasing;
yet, speaking in summary,
it is subsumed solely within "defilement associated with non-interruption."
Because this involves the conceptualization of the objects grasped through the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*),
that which exists as an illusion is the conventional,
while the fact that the illusory existence is itself emptiness is the ultimate.
The conventional is also subsumed under the defilement associated with attachment;
the ultimate is subsumed under a small portion of the meaning of emptiness within the gate of suchness.
If the conventionally existent is the conventional, [then it is so].
That which exists as an illusion is itself emptiness; both "empty" and "not empty" together constitute the True.
The conventional is subsumed as before, while the True is subsumed under the meaning of original enlightenment within the gate of birth-and-death.
It also encompasses a portion of the meaning of emptiness within the gate of True Suchness (tathatā).
If illusory existence is the conventional,
then that illusory existence is both empty and non-empty.
All phenomena take emptiness and non-emptiness as their reality.
The conventional is subsumed as before;
the ultimate is subsumed within the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
If illusion exists, that which exists as illusion is itself empty; both are termed the conventional (saṃvṛti).
That which neither exists nor is empty is the ultimate (paramārtha).
The conventional is subsumed under the meaning of non-awakening within the gate of arising and ceasing.
It also encompasses the meaning of "similar awakening" (*sādṛśa-avabodha*).
"True" (*tattva*) is subsumed under the meaning of "original awakening" (*mūla-avabodha*) within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*).
That which is illusory existence and that which is empty of illusory existence are both termed the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Neither existent nor empty—this "neither existent nor empty" nature of all phenomena is the ultimate truth.
