It is the failure to know the single true Dharma as it truly is;
thus, the characteristics of a defiled mind appear.
This refers generally to the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings and all their associated mental factors;
they all arise through the other-dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) in four aspects.
Yet, that which is eternally luminous, pure, and without change [is the perfected nature].
The mind-king and its mental factors each consist of four parts;
since they all completely take True Suchness as their essence,
True Suchness remains unchanging while following conditions.
Therefore, it is always luminous and pure.
It is like gold fashioned into various vessels;
all the vessels are nothing but gold.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, because its fundamental nature is non-conceptual," this specifically refers to the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and mental factors (*caitta*),
which likewise takes the nature of the mind as its substance.
The entirety of the mind-nature has never undergone change;
there are certainly no objects existing outside of the mind.
Because one does not awaken to the single dharma-realm,
non-associated ignorance arises through discrimination,
giving rise to all defiled minds. Regarding "non-associated ignorance":
This specifically refers to the seeds of ignorance within the eighth consciousness;
it does not correspond with the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the eighth consciousness.
This clarifies that although [this ignorance] has existed since beginningless time due to the power of ignorance, [it is distinct from its active counterparts].
It is the natural law that these eight consciousnesses and their respective mental factors each possess four parts,
extending even to all objective spheres; yet,
as for these phenomena:
Originally there is no change;
originally there is no alteration.
It remains the one true Dharma-realm.
If one can, in every thought-moment, observe that the moving mind is itself neither arising nor ceasing,
one immediately enters the gate of True Suchness (Tathatā) and thereby realizes the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
It is simply because of a momentary lapse in discernment that one fails to realize the single dharma-realm; thus,
the seeds of ignorance within the eighth consciousness [remain].
It is thus associated with the preceding seven [mental factors],
whereby active conceptualization arises,
and further, various defiled states of mind are produced.
This meaning is extremely profound and difficult to fathom;
only a Buddha can know it.
It is not something understood by others; that is to say, within the eighth consciousness,
the seeds of ignorance require only a single moment of non-awakening for their active manifestation to arise, thereby producing a defiled mind.
Although these are equal to the awakening of a bodhisattva,
they have not yet transformed the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) into the stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*), and thus have not yet exhausted its source;
this occurs only at the stage of Buddhahood.
Only when one is associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) can one penetrate to the very limits of its nature and characteristics.
This concludes the initial general clarification of the profound meaning.
Second, the detailed exposition of the sequence has two parts:
first, the formal explanation of the sequence of awakening to purity;
second, the further explanation of the meanings of correspondence and non-correspondence.
The first section has two parts:
first, clarifying the sequence of the mind free from defilement;
second, clarifying the sequence of freedom from non-awakening.
Now, first: this defiled mind produced by non-awakening has six distinct varieties.
First, the defilement associated with grasping;
[this pertains to] śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, Bodhisattvas on the stage of faith-correspondence are able to distance themselves from the defilement associated with grasping;
that is to say, the afflictions of view and thought associated with the grasping of a self.
The first fruit of the śrāvaka;
the śaikṣa stage of the pratyekabuddha;
and the bodhisattva who has resolved upon the mind through the perfection of faith.
They are all able to suddenly sever the afflictions of views and gradually sever the afflictions of thought; therefore,
it is said that they are "able to remain far removed."
Second, the defilement associated with non-interruption can be partially severed by Bodhisattvas on the stage of faith through the power of diligent cultivation.
Upon reaching the Stage of Utmost Purity, [the afflictions] are forever exhausted without remainder. Regarding "the associated defilement that is not severed":
this refers to the conceptual grasping at phenomena associated with the sixth consciousness.
It is that which is not abandoned within the teachings of the Two Vehicles.
A Bodhisattva at the stage of faith immediately studies the contemplation of mind-only consciousness.
This very attachment is being suppressed;
therefore, upon reaching the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*),
it is forever exhausted without remainder.
The defilement associated with the wisdom of discrimination extends from the stage of possessing ethical discipline up to the stage of possessing wisdom.
One can partially separate from it;
it is only upon reaching the stage of practice characterized by signlessness that it is permanently exhausted. This refers to the defilement associated with the cognition of discrimination.
This refers to the innate clinging to phenomena associated with the sixth consciousness.
Although it arises spontaneously,
it does so because one does not know, as they truly are, that all dharmas are one.
It is still called the wisdom of discernment (*viveka-jñāna*).
Second is the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), which is named "Possessing Morality" (*śīlavatī*).
The sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*),
is called "Possessing Wisdom.
The gradual abandonment of [afflictions] part by part is called "Partial Separation."
The seventh is the Far-Reaching Stage (dūramgamā bhūmiḥ), which is called "Practice Without Characteristics" (animittacaryā).
The fruit of the knowledge of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasunyatājñāna) is constantly present before one.
Therefore, this defilement is now able to be exhausted forever.
Fourth is the defilement dissociated from present form;
this is eliminated by the stage of mastery over form (*rūpavibhūti*), which has existed since beginningless time.
The habitual tendencies of falsely clinging to the distinction between the environment and its inhabitants are perfumed within the eighth consciousness.
Although it does not arise simultaneously in association with the manifesting evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*),
by the power of these seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-bīja*),
it is as yet unable to spontaneously manifest images and lands.
This is called the defilement of non-correspondence with manifested form.
Upon entering the eighth stage, the Ground of Mastery over Form,
these habitual tendencies are forever eliminated.
Therefore, the basis can manifest within the middle,
and the middle can manifest within the basis.
These five views are defilements dissociated from mind.

This state of mastery of mind is that which is eliminated; it arises from the habitual tendencies accumulated since beginningless time through the false attachment to one's own mind and the minds of others as being distinct.
It is perfumed within the eighth consciousness;
although it does not arise simultaneously in association with the manifest evolving consciousnesses,
by the power of these habit-energies (vāsanā-bīja), [the subsequent manifestations occur].
Being unable to act for the mutual benefit of self and others is called the defilement dissociated from the mind of vision.
If one enters the ninth stage, the stage of mastery over the self, [this ceases].
Then these habitual tendencies are forever eliminated; thus,
one is able to enter meditative absorption with one's own body and arise with another's body,
or enter meditative absorption with another's body and arise with one's own body.
Entering meditative absorption with one body and arising with many bodies;
entering meditative absorption with many bodies and arising with one body;
and so on, until they are fully endowed with the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
With a single voice, he universally answers all the various questions and difficulties posed by all sentient beings.
Sixth is the defilement of non-correspondence with the six fundamental karmas;
this pertains to the Bodhisattva’s stage of ultimate perfection (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*).

That which is eliminated upon entering the stage of the Tathāgata arises from the views regarding phenomena (*dharmadṛṣṭi*), attachment to phenomena (*dharmasneha*), and pride regarding phenomena (*dharma-māna*) within the seventh consciousness, which has been present since beginningless time;
it consists of the false clinging to the eighth consciousness as a real, internal self-entity.
All habitual tendencies (vāsanā) are perfumed within the eighth consciousness.
Although the power of the sixth consciousness’s fruit of the wisdom of dharma-emptiness is constantly present before it,
[the eighth consciousness] does not arise in association with the active manifestation (pravṛtti) of the seventh consciousness.
However, due to the power of these habitual tendencies and seeds,
it has not yet relinquished the designation "ripening consciousness" (vipākavijñāna),
nor has it realized the ultimate, equal, non-dual dharmakāya of all Tathāgatas.
Therefore, one must proceed from the Bodhisattva’s stage of ultimate perfection and enter the diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi) to eliminate these seeds.
This is the entry into the stage of the Tathāgata.
First, the sequence of the mind free from defilement is concluded.
Second, the sequence of freedom from non-awakening is explained. Regarding "non-awakening to the one dharma-realm":
Beginning from the stage of faith and observing the stages,
one proceeds until reaching the stage of the pure mind, where one is able to achieve a slight degree of separation [from afflictions].
Only upon entering the stage of the Tathāgata can one attain the eternal exhaustion [of ignorance].
That which fails to realize the single dharma-realm is precisely what is called the fundamental delusion of the ground-abiding ignorance (avidyāvāsabhūmi) that has no beginning.
It is constantly associated with the seventh consciousness and is also sometimes associated with the sixth consciousness;
both are what are called "delusion regarding phenomena" (dharmamoha).
It is due to this ignorance that all defiled minds arise.
The defiled minds thus produced have already been explained above.
There is a sequential order to this detachment;
therefore, I shall now further clarify the sequence of detachment from this non-awakening.
The followers of the Two Vehicles have not heard of this term "non-awakening."
How much more so regarding knowing and severing them?
Therefore, this shall not be discussed further.
In the Mahāyāna, one begins from the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).
Because one is able to observe and train in abandonment,
it is also called the Stage of Observation (vīkṣaṇā-bhūmi).
Although one still trains in abandonment, [it is so named].
One can only gradually subdue [the afflictions] but is not yet able to abandon them;
this is truly because of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation that still possess outflows (*āsrava*).
Because they have not yet been able to destroy those seeds,
one proceeds until reaching the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*),
where one becomes free from the delusion regarding phenomena (*dharma-moha*) that arises from the discrimination of the sixth consciousness.
From that point onward, one gradually becomes detached from the innate delusion regarding phenomena (*dharmaja-sahaja-moha*).
This continues until one enters the stage of a Tathāgata,
at which point the innate delusion regarding phenomena within the seventh consciousness is finally and eternally exhausted.
Because this ever-present, unique ignorance is extremely subtle,
it persists until the moment the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) manifests.
Thus, the defilements that do not correspond to the fundamental karma are extinguished simultaneously.
One should know that Bodhisattvas of the gradual teaching only understand the sequential departure from defilement.
Therefore, one must reach the Stage of Pure Mind (*śuddhabhūmi*) before being able to even slightly separate from this ignorance.
As for the Bodhisattvas of the Sudden Teaching (*tongjiao*), [they...]
From the very beginning, one should study the observation that ignorance has no inherent nature;
it is not necessary to eliminate defilements one by one,
for the ignorance that gives rise to them [is itself devoid of self-nature].
Once one has attained partial subjugation and detachment,
the defiled dharmas that arise are likewise partially eliminated;
for this reason, the initial arousal of the mind is called the "Stage of the Pure Mind."
Not only does it permanently sever the second type of defilement associated with continuity,
but it can also eliminate both the fourth and fifth types of non-associated defilements; thus,
one is able to manifest the eight phases of attaining enlightenment.
One attains mastery over form and mastery over the mind.
Question:
The previous passage stated that "due to non-awakening,
three kinds of characteristics and six kinds of characteristics arise," whereas this passage states, "because of non-awakening."
Six kinds of defilement arise.
Are these defilements identical to or distinct from their characteristics?
Furthermore, at the moment of arising,
does it arise as defiled or not?
This excludes the moment of removing defilement.
He then removed the marks of contradiction.
He replied:
"As for what is called 'marks' (lakṣaṇa)..."
This is the form of that which is universally imagined;
its substance is the dependent nature, which encompasses afflictions, karma, and suffering.
That which is called "defiled" refers to this.
This refers to the seeds and manifestations of the pervasive imagination (*parikalpa*), which,
arising from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
denote exclusively the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Defilement is like pressing upon the eye;
characteristics are like a mass of flowers.
One should simply eliminate defilement.
There is no need to eliminate these marks;
moreover, each and every mark is capable of giving rise to the six defilements.
Each and every defilement is capable of giving rise to all nine aspects; therefore,
it is absolutely impossible to specify that a particular defilement corresponds to a specific aspect.
If one considers the characteristics of the removal of defilements, they must necessarily follow the removal [of the object].
Regarding coarse discrimination, there is first, the defilement associated with grasping (*parigraha-saṃprayukta-kleśa*).
That is to say, regarding the views and afflictions within the realm of desire:
when those of the Three Vehicles abandon the delusions of view,
they simultaneously eliminate the grasping at names and other characteristics within that realm.
Furthermore, regarding the arising of the characteristics of outflowing karma (*sāsrava-karma*):

since the Noble Ones (*ārya*) certainly do not create karma for future existence, when the two vehicles exhaust their afflictions of thought (*citta-kleśa*), [they likewise do not produce such karma].
That is to say, at the time of entering nirvana, those of the two vehicles eliminate the three characteristics of the attachment to the continuity of cognition and the internal realms;
they eliminate the characteristic of suffering bound by karma within the internal realms.
Furthermore, regarding the three characteristics of karma and so forth arising based on the aggregate of suffering, there are two types of bodhisattvas.
The first is those for whom wisdom is predominant;
they relinquish birth in the realm of分段生 (segmented birth).
The various marks eliminated when born in the land of skillful means are the same as those of the two vehicles.
Second, there is the predominance of compassion.
It sustains habitual tendencies and moistens birth;
it does not eliminate the marks of cognition and the marks of continuity within the realm,
but only eliminates the marks of attachment within the realm.
Since one still takes birth through the seeds of former karma,
one likewise does not eliminate the characteristics of suffering bound by karma,
nor the three characteristics associated with karma and so forth.
However, one resolutely refrains from creating new karma;
therefore, there is no manifestation of the arising of out-flowing (āsrava) karma.
Second is the defilement associated with non-interruption.
That is, the delusions regarding the objects of perception outside the [three] realms; once these delusions are exhausted,
one partially realizes the Dharma-body.
Excluding only the fourth type of attachment to names and so forth outside the realms,
which corresponds to the defilement associated with the threefold discriminative cognition—
namely, the active afflictions (*saṃyojana*) of thought that manifest outside the realms.
Having exhausted these delusions,
one realizes the stage of signlessness and eliminates attachment to that which lies outside the [three] realms.
And it gives rise to the characteristics of untainted (anāsrava) karma involving effortful application (*sābhoga*),
yet it does not eliminate the characteristics of karma that is effortless (*anābhoga*).
Fourth, the defilement dissociated from present form (*rūpa*).
This refers to the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation regarding the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). Once these tendencies are eliminated,
one attains mastery over form (*rūpavaśitā*).
It is able to manifest all forms;
it does not exclude the characteristics of its objects.
The five views are defilements dissociated from the mind.
One then perceives the habitual tendencies of the proliferation of the subject-aspect;
having eliminated these tendencies,
one attains mastery over the mind.
It is able to manifest all minds;
it does not exclude the characteristic of being able to perceive.
Sixth, the defilements dissociated from the six fundamental karmas.
This refers precisely to the maturation-neutral seeds of karmic fruition;
once these seeds are eliminated,
there are no delusive appearances that are not completely eradicated.
One realizes the equal *dharmakāya* of all Tathāgatas;
therein, no distinct characteristics of self or other can be apprehended.
Therefore, it is said:
When one person attains Buddhahood,
the entire dharma-realm becomes the environment and the body of that single Buddha.
It is like a thousand lamps in a single room.
Each light shines everywhere;
they cannot be distinguished from one another,
yet there is no obstruction.
Nor is there any admixture.
Furthermore, only after eliminating defilement and non-awakening can the characteristics and functions of True Suchness (tathatā) be manifested.
This refers to the Dharmakāya and Sambhogakāya combined of all Tathāgatas,
which constantly and spontaneously enjoy the vast dharma-pleasure;
this is precisely the ultimate characteristic of activity.
The latter two wisdoms illuminate all phenomena;
this is precisely the ultimate ability to perceive their characteristics.
This refers to the pure consciousness associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
It is transformed into a pure Buddha-land free from outflows,
circular and boundless,
adorned with various jewels.
The body of self-enjoyment constantly dwells in reliance [upon it],
with a magnitude equal to that of the pure land.
Their physical dimensions are likewise so;
their sense faculties and marks of excellence are each and every one infinite.
This is precisely the characteristic of the ultimate realm:
the mental states of the four wisdoms are non-differentiated yet differentiated.
This is precisely the characteristic of ultimate wisdom;
it endures until the limits of the future,
neither changing nor ceasing.
This is the ultimate characteristic of continuity:
great loving-kindness and great compassion,
which embrace all sentient beings.
To be constantly free from weariness is itself the mark of ultimate attachment;
it occurs within dharmas that are devoid of names and marks.
They establish various rare sets of names, phrases,
and syllables so that all sentient beings may obtain the benefits of the four *siddhāntas*;
this is precisely the ultimate grasping of the characteristics of names and so forth.
Constantly manifesting inconceivable transformations through the three wheels;
this is the ultimate phase of the arising of karma,
flowing equally throughout the nine realms.
To sport within the hells is precisely the ultimate state of suffering bound by karma.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata is firmly able to perfectly realize the nine ultimate characteristics.
From the moment of generating the bodhicitta onwards,
one also partially realizes the nine aspects within the context of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*).
There are also nine similar aspects;
within the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā),
there are likewise nine aspects of contemplative practice (vipaśyanā).
Within the wisdom derived from hearing,
there are also nine aspects of names regarding all sentient beings.
Wherever there is principle, that is precisely the nine contemplations.
These nine contemplations are equal;
there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm.
This is the Greatness of the Essence of True Suchness (tathatā).
The three preceding aspects are the Greatness of the Characteristics of True Suchness.
The latter six characteristics are precisely the great function of True Suchness (tathatā),
for True Suchness is without division or limitation.
Because it is non-conceptual,
one may select any single characteristic from among these various characteristics.
The three great meanings of the specific characteristics, functions, and substance of non-returning can be known through the mind,
but cannot be fully expressed in words.
Yet all these do not depart from the infinitesimal mind manifest before sentient beings;
therefore, based upon this mind,
the Mahāyāna is revealed.
The first part, the correct explanation of the sequence of awakening and purification, is concluded.
Second is the secondary explanation of the meaning of correspondence and non-correspondence.
As for the meaning of correspondence:
The mind’s discrimination is distinct;
the discrimination between defilement and purity is distinct.
One knows that the characteristics of the object and the characteristics of the cognition are identical within the mind’s discrimination.
This refers to the essence of the preceding seven mind-kings (citta-rāja) as being defiled or pure;
it refers to the essence of the associated mental factors (caitta).
Since both the mind-king and its mental factors take false conceptualization as their intrinsic nature,
it is said that they are each distinct.
Each arises as a manifest activity,
and each possesses its own intrinsic nature.
Regarding the point that their characteristics are identical:

The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) that acts as the cognitive faculty is unified through conjunction; thus, the aspects of the objects of cognition appear as one. This is what is meant by "the aspects of the objects being identical."
The objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) of the object of cognition is similar to a substance and its reflection.
As for the meaning of "non-associated" (viprayukta):
"Thus, the mind is unaware; it is eternally without distinction. Regarding "the mind is unaware;

it is eternally without distinction": this refers to knowing that the characteristic of the knower and the characteristic of the object are not different. "Thus, the mind is unaware; it is eternally without distinction" means: [as explained above].
"Mind" refers to the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga) of the eighth mind-king.
"Non-enlightenment" refers to the seeds of the defiled mind.
This refers precisely to the eighth [consciousness], the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Since both the objective aspect and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) arise based upon the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*),
it is said that they are not distinct from one another.
Regarding the knowledge that their characteristics differ:
the eighth consciousness’s manifest seeing-part is the subject that performs the cognition.
Therefore, although there is cognition,
the seeds of the defiled mind do not arise as actual manifestations; thus,
it is incapable of taking [them] as objects.
Therefore, there is no cognition.
Regarding the fact that the conditions and characteristics differ: this refers to the eighth [consciousness's] seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*).
The seeds of defiled minds take the three categories of natures as their objects;
however, [the seeds of] uncontaminated minds have no objects of perception.
The second part, the detailed demonstration of the sequence, is concluded.
Third, regarding the summary that identifies the two obstacles as defiled minds:
this refers to the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Because it obstructs the fundamental wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness), this summarizes the six types of defiled minds,
all of which are termed afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
These consist of the various delusions associated with the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*).
All these are termed the afflictions of view and thought within the realm;
they are able to obstruct the true suchness of self-emptiness and consist of various delusions associated with the clinging to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).
Excluding only the single category of delusion regarding phenomena (*dharmamoha*),
all others are termed the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) outside the realm;
they are able to obstruct the true suchness of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā-tathatā*).
Only fundamental wisdom can realize suchness;
since [these afflictions] obstruct suchness, [they must be abandoned].
This is precisely what obstructs fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).
Because it obstructs the knowledge of mastery over worldly activities, only that single type of delusion regarding phenomena (*dharmamoha*) is designated as "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
By means of this delusion regarding phenomena...
To lack mastery over worldly karma is called an obstruction to that wisdom.
What is the meaning of this?
Because it relies on a defiled mind that clings to the immeasurable false objects of the grasper and the grasped,
it contradicts the nature of equality of all phenomena; this explains why the defiled mind is able to obstruct fundamental wisdom.
The nature of equality of all phenomena is precisely suchness,
which fundamentally lacks both subject and object;
this is the nature of all phenomena.
It is equal and quiescent,
without the characteristic of arising;
it is ignorance and lack of awakening.
Delusion contradicts awakening;

therefore, regarding the various objects of the world and their diverse karmic functions, one is entirely unable to know them as they truly are. This explains why ignorance is able to obstruct sovereign wisdom.
Only by knowing things as they truly are can one attain mastery; thus ends the second section,
which clarifies the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing.
Third, the discernment of the characteristics of arising and ceasing, in two parts:
first, the formal analysis;
second, the resolution of doubts through questions and answers.
First: Furthermore,
in analyzing the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the mind,
there are two distinct types.
First is the coarse,
which refers to the associated mind;
second is the subtle.
That which is non-associated with the mind, yet arises in association with the mind, is called "associated mind.
This refers precisely to the manifestation of the primary mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta).
What is called arising, abiding, and ceasing in the *Laṅkāvatāra* does not arise in association with the mind;
it is termed "non-associated mind" (*viprayukta-citta*),
which refers precisely to the seeds of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
This refers to what is called the "streaming" of arising, abiding, and ceasing in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
It is the coarsest among the coarse;
it is the cognitive domain of the wisdom of ordinary beings—the coarsest among the coarse.
This refers precisely to the defilement associated with the first grasping (*prathama-grāha-saṃprayukta-kleśa*).
It is that which has originally been abandoned by those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) and by Bodhisattvas on the stage of faith (*adhimukti-bhūmi*).
The present mention of it as "the cognitive sphere of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana-jñāna-viṣaya*) is [for this reason].
The stage of faith is termed the "inner ordinary" (ābhyantarapṛthagjana);
its wisdom and abandonment are identical to those of the followers of the two vehicles,
as it has not yet entered the noble stages of the Mahāyāna.
The subtle within the coarse,
and the coarse within the subtle, constitute the cognitive domain of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom.
The subtle within the subtle.

This is the realm of the Buddha’s wisdom. [The eight characters "is the treasury within" are missing; they are supplemented here according to the Liang edition. The coarse within the subtle refers to the defilement associated with non-interruption (*asaṃdhini-kleśa*).
The defilement associated with the wisdom of discrimination is the coarse within the subtle;
it is precisely the defilement dissociated from the manifest form.
The Bodhisattva who sees the defilements as dissociated from the mind refers to those from the Stage of Pure Mind (śuddhacitta-bhūmi) upward.
The subtlest of the subtle refers to the fundamental afflictions dissociated from karma;
these can be known only by the Buddha's wisdom.
Thus one is able to illuminate its source.
These two kinds of characteristics— the coarse and the subtle—
both arise through the power of the permeation of ignorance (*avidyā*).
However, as for their basis in causes and conditions,
the cause is non-awakening.
These are conditions arising from delusory objects.
When the causes cease, the conditions cease;
because the conditions cease, the corresponding mind ceases.
Because the cause ceases, the non-associated mind ceases; "ignorance" here refers exclusively to delusion regarding phenomena (*dharmamoha*),
as all other factors are subsumed under the category of afflicted minds.
Non-awakening is precisely the delusion of the dharma of ignorance;
when its conditions cease, it does not arise as active manifestation.
Therefore, the associated mind ceases;
because its cause has ceased, it no longer possesses seeds.
Thus, the dissociated mind ceases.
Thus one becomes a Tathāgata.
Question:
Since it is said that "when causes cease, conditions cease," [how is this so?]
Thus, before one has attained Buddhahood,
ignorance has not yet been extinguished,
and the objective realm has necessarily not yet been extinguished.
Since the object has not yet ceased,
the corresponding mind should likewise not cease; how,
then, can one reach the stage of signlessness?
"Is defilement associated with cessation already exhausted?
Answer: "Ignorance is twofold."
First, that which co-exists with the seventh consciousness is exhausted only at the stage of Buddhahood;
second, that which co-exists with the sixth consciousness—
It is further divided into two:
first, conceptual discrimination, which is eliminated at the Stage of the Pure Mind (śuddhacitta-bhūmi).
The second is that which is co-nascent;
it excludes the stage of signlessness and ceases the portion of ignorance.
Then the objects also cease partially;
because the objects cease partially,
the associated mind also ceases partially.
Furthermore, this so-called "cessation of the associated mind" refers only to the cessation of the manifestation of defiled minds;
as for the manifestation of the untainted [mind], it is not so.
Thus, the four wisdoms of the Buddha-fruit are all associated with twenty-one dharmas,
and they are never again extinguished.
What is called the cessation of the dissociated mind refers merely to the cessation of the seeds of outflows (āsrava); as for the untainted seeds (anāsrava-bīja), [they do not cease].
It is then perpetually sustained by the āmala-vijñāna,
never ceasing until the end of the future.
The first section, the Correct Analysis, is concluded.
Second, the Question-and-Answer Explanation of Doubts:
"If the mind were to cease," [it would follow that...]
What is continuity? If there is continuity, how can one speak of cessation?
This is intended precisely to demonstrate that the seeds and manifestations of the defiled mind are capable of being extinguished.
Because the seeds and manifestations of the pure mind do not perish,
he poses a question to initiate the discussion.
He answers:
Indeed it is so.
What is now called "cessation" refers merely to the cessation of mental characteristics.
It is not that the substance of the mind perishes; "mental characteristics" refers specifically to defiled characteristics, while "the substance of the mind" refers to the essence itself.
This refers to the fundamental substance that is the basis for both defilement and purity, yet is itself neither defiled nor pure.
Defilement also relies upon this substance,
because it is in opposition to it.
It is merely called a characteristic;
purity also has characteristics,
namely, the characteristic of the greatness of True Suchness (tathatā).
Because it accords with the essence,
it is directly named the "essence" itself;
it is like water [stirred] by the wind.
Yet there is the characteristic of motion;
because the wind is extinguished, the characteristic of motion is likewise extinguished.
It is not that the substance of water ceases.
If the water were to cease,
then its movement would necessarily be severed.
Because water that has no basis lacks the movement that depends upon it,
and because the essence of water does not perish while its characteristic of movement continues, water is used as a metaphor for the essence of the mind.
The wind is a metaphor for ignorance;
it moves.
This is an analogy for the characteristics of the mind.
Sentient beings are likewise;
by the power of ignorance, they [are thus].
This causes the mind to move;
because ignorance is extinguished, the characteristic of movement is likewise extinguished.
It is not that the substance of the mind is extinguished; if the mind were to be extinguished,
then sentient beings would be annihilated.
Because there is nothing upon which to rely and no one who relies, ignorance causes the mind to move,
just as wind gives rise to waves.
Thus, the eight consciousnesses and all their associated mental factors are all states of movement;
because ignorance has ceased, [they cease as well].
The characteristics of defilement and movement cease;
it is not the essence of the mind that ceases,
just as when the wind subsides, the waves cease.
The substance of water does not perish;
thus, the mental states associated with the four wisdoms are all like water.
If the extinction of the mind meant the annihilation of sentient beings,
then the Tathāgata would not be called the unsurpassed among sentient beings;
for [he possesses] the essence of the four wisdom-minds which have no basis.

Thus, there is no conventionally designated Tathāgata that can serve as a basis [for such a designation], because the essence of mind is indestructible and the movement of mind continues in succession. (The Liang commentary states: "Because the essence of mind is not extinguished, the movement of mind continues."
Because the substance does not perish,
the mind attains continuity;
it is solely because delusion ceases that [this occurs].
The characteristics of the mind perish along with it;
it is not that the wisdom of the mind perishes.
This text indicates that only defiled characteristics are extinguished.
It is named "the Immovable.
Furthermore, the four categories of wisdom and mind are precisely the great aspect of the true suchness (tathatā).
The continuous arising of the function of True Suchness (tathatā) may still be termed the "succession of mental movement. However,
because one realizes that movement occurs within non-movement, movement possesses no characteristic of movement.
It is not the same as the functioning within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
it cannot be conceived or measured by the mind, intellect, or consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*) of any sentient being.
This concludes the initial clarification of defilement and purity, and of arising and ceasing.
*The Lianwang Shu (Tearing the Net Commentary) on the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, Scroll Three;
*The Lianwang Shu on the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, Scroll Four.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Ouyi of Lingfeng, Zhixu.

Second, the clarification of the perfuming of defilement and purity, in four parts: first, a general presentation of the meaning of perfuming; second, an explanation of the perfuming of defiled phenomena;
third, an explanation of the perfuming of pure phenomena.
Fourth, the determination of what is severed and what is not severed. First:
furthermore, by the power of the perfuming of four kinds of dharmas.
Defiled and pure phenomena arise without interruption;
there is but one pure phenomenon.
The first is suchness;
the second is the cause of defilement,
namely, ignorance.
The three deluded minds refer to the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
The four deluded objects refer to the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). The one pure dharma refers to *tathatā* (suchness).
In short, all untainted seeds in their active state,
as well as the rational nature that serves as the basis for the mind and mental factors,
are collectively termed *tathatā* (suchness).
In essence, rationality is indeed suchness;
and because the outflow-free seeds and manifestations accord with suchness, they are so designated.
This is also what is termed *tathatā* (suchness).
Regarding the second point, the "cause of defilement" referred to as ignorance (*avidyā*),
it refers exclusively to non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*).
This refers to the delusion (*moha*) associated with the seventh consciousness, which is both constantly active and unshared (*asādhāraṇa*),
as well as that which is solitary and unshared.
This refers to the ignorance that deludes regarding the principle (tattva), which is associated with the sixth consciousness;
it may be either discriminative (vikalpita) or innate (sahaja).
It serves as the basis for all defiled phenomena;
therefore, it is called the "cause of defilement.
Third, regarding the deluded mind, it refers to the *karmic consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*).
This refers generally to the essence of the eight consciousnesses and the essence of their associated mental factors (caitta), which, based upon them,
are able to give rise to the two divisions of subject (darśana-bhāga) and object (nimitta-bhāga).
Because it involves movement and transformation,
it is called "karma" (action).
Regarding the four delusive objects, they refer to the six sense-fields (ṣaḍāyatana).
This refers generally to the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of both mind and mental factors;
in total, it does not transcend the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*),
which are precisely the *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition).
As for the meaning of perfuming (vāsanā):
it is like a worldly garment that is neither foul-smelling nor fragrant.
If one fumigates it with various substances, it takes on their respective scents; yet the clothing itself is neither foul nor fragrant.
This serves as a metaphor for the nature that remains unchanging while following conditions.
Fundamentally, it is neither defiled nor pure.
When perfumed by foul substances,
it then possesses a foul odor.
This is an analogy for the unchanging nature which,
following defiled conditions,
manifests defiled characteristics.
When incensed with fragrant substances,
it emits a fragrance;
this is a metaphor for the unchanging nature.
In accordance with pure conditions,
there is the function of purity;
such is the pure dharma of *tathatā*.
The nature is not defiled;
however, due to the permeation of ignorance, it manifests the appearance of defilement. This is the true suchness of the virtues of the nature.
Although it is neither defiled nor pure,
because it is free from defilement,
it is provisionally termed a pure dharma.
It is like an unstained garment;
this refers to the consciousness that is unobscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta),
which is fundamentally the entirety of true suchness (tathatā).
Therefore, it is precisely named *tathatā* (suchness).
As for the statement that "defiled characteristics exist because of the permeation of ignorance," this refers to the defiled seeds from which [the characteristics] are perfumed.
The manifestation of defiled phenomena arises,
as fully explained in the preceding text regarding the three characteristics and six aspects. This refers to the characteristic of the defilement of ignorance.
In reality, there is no pure karma;
it is because of the permeation of True Suchness that its pure function is said to exist. As for the defiled characteristics of ignorance:
This refers generally to the mind and mental factors arising from ignorance;
it is also that which is constituted by the entire substance of true thusness (tathatā),
and its nature is neither defiled nor pure.
Because they have already been permeated by defilement—
just like a foul-smelling garment—
they possess no pure karma.
Regarding "because it is permeated by True Suchness":
this means that one perfumes it with the pure dharmas of cultivated merit that are free from outflows,
just as one perfumes a foul-smelling garment with incense.
To speak of having a pure function is like how,
by first eliminating foul odors,
the function of fragrance is then revealed.
That which possesses the characteristic of defilement must necessarily possess the function of defilement;
and the function of defilement causes one to transmigrate through birth and death.
The faults are profound and grave;
therefore, I shall not speak of them.
Indeed, there is a pure function.
There must be pure characteristics;
yet these pure characteristics are darkly merged with the pure essence,
beyond the measurement of the world.
Therefore, it is not discussed here.
First, the general presentation of the meaning of perfuming (vāsanā) is concluded.
Second, the explanation of the perfuming of defiled phenomena is twofold.
First, the primary elucidation of the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*);
second, the explanation of its specific distinctions.
Now, the first.
How is it that the perfuming of defiled dharmas is not severed?
It is because, based upon true thusness (tathatā), ignorance arises.
It serves as the cause for all defilements;
furthermore, this ignorance perfumes the True Suchness (tathatā).
Once it has been perfumed,
the mind of deluded thought arises;
this is the mind of deluded thought.
It further perfumes ignorance;
because of this perfuming,
one does not awaken to the true Dharma.
Because of non-awakening,
the appearances of delusive objects manifest;
this occurs due to the power of the habitual perfuming of the delusive mind.
Giving rise to various forms of attachment to distinctions,
they perform various karmas and undergo the retributive fruits of manifold physical and mental sufferings; thus it has been for sentient beings since beginningless time.
By the nature of phenomena, there are eight kinds of consciousness.
These eight kinds of consciousness and their associated mental factors are,
in reality, without distinction in their characteristics.
Its essence is precisely the one Dharma-realm,
also named True Suchness (tathatā).
True Suchness serves as the basis for both delusion and awakening.

Because it has never been awakened since beginningless time, the seventh consciousness gives rise to the ignorance that deludes regarding principle; it does not know that the true Dharma is fundamentally one.
Therefore, it is said that ignorance arises in dependence upon *tathatā* (suchness).
It serves as the cause for all defilements.
If one were to claim that True Suchness (tathatā) must first exist before ignorance (avidyā) arises, [that would be incorrect].
Due to the existence of ignorance,
there is the ālayavijñāna; due to the existence of the ālayavijñāna, [there is ignorance].
If there were previously the seven evolving consciousnesses,
then sentient beings would have a beginning;
how would this differ from the non-Buddhist view that primordial darkness gave rise to cognition?
Now, regarding this ignorance that perfumes the True Suchness:
it means that the manifestation of a single moment of ignorance immediately perfumes the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
It forms the seed of ignorance.
The essence of the ālayavijñāna is precisely suchness (tathatā).
It is, for example, like water when it is stirred.
This immediately activates the moist nature;
therefore, it is said that [ignorance] perfumes the *tathatā*.
This is stated with respect to the non-difference between consciousness and *tathatā*.
However, although water is in motion, its moist nature does not change; this is the essence that remains unchanging while following conditions (*pratyaya*).
Based on this principle, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* further states that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is not perfumed.
This is stated in terms of consciousness and true suchness (tathatā) not being identical;
it serves precisely to mutually manifest the subtle principle and involves no contradiction or obstruction.
Once the perfuming has occurred and the deluded mind arises,
it relies upon the gate of arising and ceasing;
because it is conventional, its characteristics are distinct.
Thus, there are the eight consciousnesses and their various mental factors (caitta),
which possess four aspects in terms of essence and function,
and differ according to the distinction between seeds and manifestations.
Yet these distinctions are all devoid of intrinsic nature;
they exist solely due to ignorance.
Failing to realize the absence of intrinsic nature,
one gives rise to the differentiated dharma-attachment associated with the sixth consciousness;
this is termed the "deluded thought-mind."
Regarding this deluded mind further perfuming ignorance:
within the eighth consciousness,
there already exist the seeds of innate ignorance.
It causes the seventh consciousness to give rise,
moment by moment, to the active manifestation of ignorance that is deluded regarding the principle;
meanwhile, this sixth consciousness gives rise to the active manifestation of the false conceptualization of grasping at phenomena as real.
It perfumes the eighth fundamental consciousness,
thereby spontaneously forming the seeds of deluded thought,
and furthermore, it assists the power of the seeds of ignorance.
Therefore, this is precisely what is called "perfuming ignorance.
Because of this perfuming, one fails to awaken to the true Dharma;
this arises from delusion regarding the Dharma.
Furthermore, it gives rise to self-delusion and so forth.
As for the appearance of the characteristics of false objects due to non-awakening,
this occurs because of self-delusion.
This manifests as the realms of the six sense objects within the segmented birth-and-death of the triple world.
Due to the power of the habitual perfuming of the deluded mind,
various forms of differentiated attachment arise.
These refer to the various afflictions of view and thought, both within and beyond the realms.
"Creating various kinds of karma" refers to outflowing wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable karma.
The "outflow-free" (anāsrava) refers to the karma of partial truth and so forth.
The "reception of various fruits of suffering, such as body and mind," refers to the two types of birth and death: the fragmented (paricchinna) and the transformative (pariṇāma).
Although the three— delusion, karma, and suffering—
revolve in an unceasing cycle,
when one investigates their ultimate root and origin:
Cessation arises solely from ignorance’s delusion regarding the true dharma-realm;
yet ignorance has no inherent substance,
for it is not separate from the nature of true suchness and original enlightenment.
It is like a person who sleeps and dreams;
within the dream, they undergo immeasurable cycles of saṃsāra,
only to suddenly wake from their sleep.
Emptiness has nothing to be attained.
If there is no mind during the time of waking,
how could there be a dreaming mind?
If one does not investigate this dreaming mind,
where else could one seek the mind of the waking state? Second,
the distinction in the interpretation of the meaning of the perfuming of delusive objects.
There are two kinds of distinctions:
first, the perfuming that increases conceptual differentiation;
second, the perfuming that increases grasping. False objects fundamentally manifest only as the mind.
Due to this lack of understanding,
it in turn perfumes the mind,
first increasing the perfuming of discrimination.
The former assists both the delusions of view within and outside the realm of existence (*dhātu*),
while the latter, the increase of grasping and perfuming,
assists only the delusions of thought (*vitarka*) within the realm of existence.
If it assists the views and afflictions within the realm,
it prevents ordinary beings from emerging from birth and death;
if it assists the delusions of view outside the realm...
It causes those of the two vehicles to swiftly seek nirvana.
Furthermore, the meaning of the perfuming of the deluded mind is also divided into two distinct types.
First, it increases the perfuming of the fundamental karmic consciousness,
causing arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas to undergo the suffering of birth and extinction.
Second, it increases the perfuming of the discriminative consciousness of phenomena.
It causes all ordinary beings to undergo the suffering of being bound by karma; within the realms, they increase their karma-consciousness through views and afflictions,
thereby undergoing the birth and death of transformation.
This is called the suffering of arising and ceasing;
within the realms, it causes the views and afflictions to increase and the phenomenal consciousness to flourish.
Experiencing分段生死 (segmented birth and death) is termed the suffering bound by karma;
this is the meaning of the permeation of ignorance.
There are also two kinds of distinctions:
first, fundamental perfuming,
which establishes the meaning of the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).

The second is the perfuming of views and craving, which accomplishes the meaning of the *vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of objects). Ignorance regarding phenomena (*dharma-moha*) is called fundamental perfuming;
ignorance regarding self (*ātma-moha*) is called the perfuming of views and craving.
The second [section] concludes the explanation of the perfuming of defiled dharmas.
The third [section] explains the perfuming of pure dharmas in two parts;
first, the explicit clarification of the meaning of perfuming.
Second, the differentiation of the meanings of the commentary; first:
How is it that the perfuming of pure dharmas is uninterrupted?
It means that True Suchness perfumes ignorance.
By the power of the causes and conditions of habitual perfuming,
it causes the deluded mind to grow weary of the suffering of birth and death and to seek the bliss of nirvana.
By means of these causes and conditions of aversion and seeking arising from this deluded mind,
one further perfumes the *tathatā* (suchness). Because of this perfuming, [the transformation occurs].
Then one gains confidence that within one's own body there is the *tathatā* dharma,
which is pure by nature,
and knows all objective realms.
It is only the deluded movement of the mind;
ultimately, it does not exist at all.
Because one can know this thus, according to reality.
One cultivates the dharma of seclusion and gives rise to various concordant practices,
remaining free from all conceptual discrimination.
Without any grasping or attachment,
they pass through immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas by virtue of the power of habitual practice.
Ignorance is extinguished.
Because ignorance is extinguished,
the characteristics of the mind do not arise.
Because the mind does not arise,
the appearances of objects are extinguished;
thus are all causes and conditions of defilement.
Furthermore, when the mental characteristics of the fruit of defilement are entirely extinguished,
it is called attaining nirvāṇa;
one then accomplishes various sovereign activities and the true thusness (*tathatā*).
This refers to the untainted seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as well as the superior functions within the fruition of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
both of these accord with the *dharmatā* of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, all are termed *tathatā* (Suchness).
The internal permeation of seeds acts as the cause,
while the external permeation of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas acts as the condition.
These internal causes and external conditions do not depart from the momentary mind manifesting before sentient beings;
by means of this mind-nature, [they arise].
Because there are truly no external objects;
for the beginningless untainted seeds are not separate from the nature of the present mind.

This is because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions have all realized that the nature of the minds of sentient beings does not exist outside of the nature of the minds of sentient beings.
Regarding the statement that "verbal expression perfumes ignorance":
first, there is the external perfuming by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
which perfumes the sixth consciousness as well as the five sensory consciousnesses.
Causing them to see forms,
hear sounds,
and smell fragrances.
While reciting and chanting,
their bodies were bathed in light,
or their heads were stroked by hands.
Or, when clothing covers the body,
the mental consciousness experiences it;
through this active manifestation, seeds are perfumed and formed.
Second, the internal perfuming of the untainted seeds causes one to believe and accept [the teachings],
such that one neither doubts nor slanders them.

To cause the mind of deluded thought to loathe the suffering of birth and death and seek the bliss of nirvana is precisely to give rise to the outflowing wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
By means of these causes and conditions of loathing and seeking with this deluded mind, one further perfumes the True Suchness.
This refers to the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation that are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Internally, they increase the power of the seeds of the untainted (*anāsrava*);
externally, they evoke the compassion of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
"Having confidence that one's own person possesses the Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā)" refers to the arousal of the mind through the perfection of faith.
"Because one is able to know it thus, in accordance with reality," and so forth.
The arousal of the mind through practice and understanding;
"without conceptual discrimination," etc.,
refers to the arousal of the mind through realization.
The phrase "because ignorance ceases, the characteristics of the mind do not arise," and so forth,
serves as proof of the Buddha’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
"Accomplishing various differentiated activities" refers to...
This refers to the Buddha’s subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Second, the differentiation of the meanings of the two explanations.
First, the explanation of the differentiation of the meaning of delusive perfuming.
Second, the distinct meanings of the two types of true permeation (*tathatā-vāsanā*). First:
there are two kinds of meaning regarding the permeation of the deluded mind (*mṛṣā-citta*).
First, the discerning consciousness perfumes [the storehouse consciousness],
causing all ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles to feel weary of the suffering of birth and death.
According to one's capacity,
one proceeds toward the unsurpassed path;
this is the second type of mental perfuming.
It causes all bodhisattvas to arouse a courageous mind and swiftly enter non-abiding nirvana. Regarding the first type, that which is perfumed by the consciousness that discerns phenomena:
this refers to those who uphold the common teachings of the three vehicles.
They do not understand the seventh and eighth consciousnesses,
but merely cultivate the contemplation of the emptiness of persons with the sixth mental consciousness,
thereby destroying the afflictions of views and thoughts to attain nirvana.
Alternatively, there are those who uphold the gradual teachings of the Mahāyāna;
although they understand the seventh and eighth consciousnesses,
because their afflictions of views and thought are heavy, [they do not realize them].
Out of fear of birth and death,
one first relies upon the sixth consciousness to cultivate the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*),
and subsequently cultivates the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that one proceeds according to one's capacity.
Nevertheless, both these ordinary beings (bāla) and those on the stages of the noble ones (ārya) are indeed directed toward Bodhi.
That is to say, even those of the two vehicles must necessarily enter the ultimate reality by means of the provisional; therefore,
it is said collectively that they "proceed toward the unsurpassed path."
Regarding the second type of mental permeation, it refers to those bodhisattvas of gradual teaching who have entered the stage of the pure mind-ground and transformed the seventh consciousness.
This causes them to correspond with the wisdom of equality and to flow spontaneously into the ocean of great nirvana;
or [it applies to] those who are bodhisattvas of the sudden teaching.
From the very beginning, one contemplates that the moving mind is itself neither arising nor ceasing;
thus, one immediately enters the gate of True Suchness (tathatā).
This is what is meant by being able to contemplate all deluded thoughts as being without marks (animitta).
This constitutes the realization of the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
although this observing mind is still the sixth consciousness, it is so designated.
And because it takes fundamental ignorance as its object of contemplation, it is called "mental permeation.
Second, the distinct meanings of the two types of true permeation are explained. Third.
First, the heading;
second, the explanation;
third, the concluding judgment.
First, regarding the meaning of the permeation of the true mind,
there are likewise two distinct types.
First, the permeation of the essence;
second, the permeation of the function. This very essence of the mind-nature, True Suchness, is common to both Buddhas and sentient beings.
They are equal and non-dual.
Although they are fundamentally non-dual, there are individual Buddhas and individual sentient beings.
Even down to each and every atom,
each one takes True Suchness (tathatā) in its entirety as its essence;
it is not merely a small portion of True Suchness.
Although for each and every Buddha,
each and every sentient being,
and even down to each and every minute particle of dust.
This is the entire substance of True Suchness (*tathatā*);
yet, there are not multiple instances of True Suchness.
This is the inconceivable Dharma-gate of the One Mind.
It is like a thousand lamps illuminating together;
they mutually pervade and mutually contain one another,
without confusion and without obstruction.
Therefore, according to the Buddha’s words,
all sentient beings are equally beings within the Buddha’s own mind.
Because the Buddha-mind extends vertically through the past and future and pervades horizontally throughout all space, such that nothing exists outside of it;
speaking in terms of sentient beings,
this refers to all Buddhas.
These are all the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings;
because the minds of sentient beings extend vertically through time and horizontally across space,
there is nothing external to them.
If we consider only this present, momentary thought and speech,
then all Buddhas and all sentient beings [are contained therein].
Furthermore, these are the Buddhas born from within my own mind;
by means of this present, infinitesimal moment of mind, they extend vertically through all time and pervade horizontally throughout all space.
Because there is nothing external,
this is called the non-differentiation of the three: mind, Buddha, and sentient beings.
Therefore, the untainted seeds inherently present within the ālayavijñāna are the very substance of the True Suchness (tathatā) of my own mind;
they constitute the internal cause for its manifestation.
This is called "substantial permeation.
The great functioning of the compassion of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas at the stage of fruition is precisely the functioning of the True Suchness of my own mind.
External conditions providing assistance is called "perfuming through function. Generally speaking, the terms "internal" and "external" are all spoken according to conventional usage.
It does not exist apart from the mind.
There are two explanations,
the first of which explains the permeation of the essence (*tixun*).
Second, the explanation of the function of perfuming.
This section has two parts.
First, the direct explanation.

Second, the resolution of doubts. First, regarding the "substantial permeation" (tixun): [The text continues: ...the substantial permeation refers to the Tathāgatagarbha, which is the fundamental cause for the manifestation of all Buddha-dharmas. It is like the waxing moon; as it gradually increases, it eventually becomes full. This is called the "substantial permeation. As for the "functional permeation" (yixun), it refers to the permeation by the Mahāyāna teachings. It is like the light of the sun and moon, which can illuminate all things. This is called the "functional permeation. Furthermore, the substantial permeation is the internal cause, while the functional permeation is the external condition. Because these two causes and conditions are present, the pure dharmas of the Buddha-nature gradually increase until they reach fulfillment. This is called the "permeation of the nature of phenomena" (faxing xun). As for the "permeation of the practice" (xingxiu xun), it refers to the permeation of the six sense organs through the cultivation of the Mahāyāna teachings. Because the six sense organs are permeated by the Mahāyāna teachings, the seeds of the Buddha-dharmas within them gradually increase until they reach fulfillment. This is called the "permeation of the practice. Furthermore, the permeation of the nature of phenomena is the cause, while the permeation of the practice is the fruit. Because these two causes and fruits are present, one attains the stage of Buddhahood. This is called the "permeation of the fruit. Furthermore, the permeation of the nature of phenomena is the permeation of the true thusness (zhenru), while the permeation of the practice is the permeation of the consciousnesses. Because the true thusness permeates the consciousnesses, the seeds of the Buddha-dharmas within the consciousnesses gradually increase until they reach fulfillment. This is called the "permeation of the consciousnesses. Furthermore, the permeation of the nature of phenomena is the permeation of the object, while the permeation of the practice is the permeation of the subject. Because the object permeates the subject, the seeds of the Buddha-dharmas within the subject gradually increase until they reach fulfillment. This is called the "permeation of the subject. Furthermore, the permeation of the nature of phenomena is the permeation of the dharma-realm, while the permeation of the practice is the permeation of the wisdom. Because the dharma-realm permeates the wisdom, the seeds of the Buddha-dharmas within the wisdom gradually increase until they reach fulfillment. This is called the "permeation of the wisdom. Furthermore, the permeation of the nature of phenomena is the permeation of the principle, while the permeation of the practice is the permeation of the phenomenon. Because the principle permeates the phenomenon, the seeds of the Buddha-dharmas within the phenomenon gradually increase until they reach fulfillment. This is called the "permeation of the phenomenon. Furthermore, the permeation of the nature of phenomena is the permeation of the unconditioned, while the permeation of the practice is the permeation of the conditioned. Because the unconditioned permeates the conditioned, the seeds of the Buddha-dharmas within the conditioned gradually increase until they reach fulfillment. This is called the "permeation of the conditioned. Furthermore, the permeation of the nature of phenomena is the permeation of the ultimate truth, while the permeation of the practice is the permeation of the conventional truth. Because the ultimate truth permeates the conventional truth, the seeds of the Buddha-dharmas within the conventional truth gradually increase until they reach fulfillment. This is called the "permeation of the conventional truth.
