they depend upon the essence of True Suchness.
Because it is inherently endowed with such true qualities and characteristics,
ordinary beings remain unaware of them in their daily lives;
thus, it is merely termed the *tathāgatagarbha*.
In terms of the Buddhas' emergence from obstructions and their perfect clarity,
it is re-designated as the *dharmakāya*.
This concludes the initial section on the correct manifestation.
Second, resolving doubts:
It was stated above that True Suchness is free from all marks;
why is it now said that it is fully endowed with all marks of merit? It was stated above that True Suchness is free from all marks.
This refers precisely to the meaning explained within the Gate of True Suchness (tathatā-mukha). Answer:
Although it truly possesses all merits, [it is so described].
Yet there is no mark of differentiation;
all those phenomena are of one single flavor.
"Single reality" means being free from the marks of conceptual differentiation,
because it is non-dual in nature. "Of one single flavor" means...
They are identical in being untainted and savorless.
"Identical in being the one true" refers to suchness and the wisdom of suchness.
This is precisely the single true dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*).
As for being free from the marks of conceptual discrimination,
it cannot be fathomed or cognized by ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles, or bodhisattvas at the stage of provisional capacity.
Regarding "because of non-duality," this refers exclusively to what is subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This is because [the other two natures] depend upon the characteristics of arising and ceasing within the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) and so forth.
And how are all those various differentiated characteristics established?
They are established by means of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
Originally, it is mind-only;
in reality, there is no discrimination.
It is because of non-awakening that [discrimination arises].
When the discriminating mind arises and perceives the existence of objective realms,
this is called ignorance; yet, the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure.

Because ignorance does not arise, it is precisely within suchness that the meaning of the great light of wisdom is established. If the mind gives rise to views regarding objects, then there is the characteristic of non-seeing;
however, the nature of the mind is without seeing.
Thus, there is nothing that is not seen; for this reason, the meaning of the "all-illuminating dharma-realm" is established within True Suchness (tathatā).
If the mind were to move, it would not be true comprehension.
It is not intrinsically pure;
it is not permanent, blissful, self, or pure;
it is not quiescent.
This is transformation;
it is not autonomous.
Because of this, there arise false and defiled states exceeding the sands of the Ganges; yet, because the nature of the mind is immovable, the meaning of "true realization" is thereby established.
This refers to the meaning of the characteristics of pure merit exceeding the sands of the Ganges.

If the mind arises, seeing other objects that can be conceptually distinguished and sought, then there will be a deficiency regarding internal dharmas; yet, by means of boundless merit, [this deficiency is overcome].
This is precisely the self-nature of the one mind;
one does not perceive any other dharma that could be further sought.
Therefore, it is fully endowed with inconceivable dharmas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, which are neither different nor identical.

Because it is never interrupted by virtue of its inherently possessed qualities and characteristics, True Suchness is called the Tathāgatagarbha; and because one realizes these inherently possessed qualities and characteristics, it is also termed the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata. Thus, the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition.
It is called the Tathāgatagarbha;
it may also be termed the Dharmakāya as the Principle.
Thus, the fruition penetrates to the source of the cause.
It is called the Dharma-body,
and it may also be called the ultimate Tathāgatagarbha.
This concludes the initial section on the manifestation of its essence and characteristics.
Second, the manifestation of its function has three parts:
first, the explicit clarification of the function, which is suchness itself;
second, the extensive clarification of the differences in perception according to the capacities of sentient beings.
The third section demonstrates the wondrous function of True Suchness (*tathatā*). First:
Furthermore, as for the function of True Suchness:
This refers to when all Buddhas, while on the stage of the causal ground,
gave rise to great compassion and practiced the various perfections, the four means of attraction, and other such deeds.
Observing all beings as identical to oneself,
one universally delivers and liberates them throughout the bounds of the future.
Without being limited by the number of kalpas,
one understands as it truly is the equality of self and others,
yet does not grasp at the marks of sentient beings.
By means of such great wisdom of skillful means,
one extinguishes beginningless ignorance and realizes the fundamental Dharma-body.
Spontaneously giving rise to inconceivable karma,
its various sovereign and differentiated activities pervade the entire dharma-realm.
It is equal to suchness,
yet no characteristic of utility can be apprehended therein. Why is this?
All Tathāgatas are solely the Dharma-body, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
and possess no worldly realm or activity. As for all Buddhas while they were on the stage of practice (caryā-bhūmi):
This was precisely when he was equal to us as an ordinary person;
by believing that the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma exists within his own mind,
he was able to give rise to great compassion and the four great vows.
They practice the six perfections, the four means of integration,
and other such deeds, universally saving all sentient beings throughout the entirety of all kalpas.
This is precisely the practice of the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), through which one realizes as it truly is the equality of self and others,
yet without grasping at the marks of sentient beings;
this is the practice of the gate of tranquility (*śamatha*).
The two gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā must be practiced in tandem; this is further explained in the subsequent section on practicing within faith.
This was based on the merit of one's own practice;
therefore, *śamatha* (calm abiding) was explained first.
The present text, however, is intended to reveal the function of transforming others.
Therefore, the contemplation is clarified first.
Furthermore, once one has contemplated the identity of all things herein,
one then gives rise to the vast mind within Prajñā.
To universally rescue and liberate all beings is to give rise to the first resolve within Prajñā;
it is to thoroughly understand the equality of self and others.
That is, within *prajñā*, one gives rise to love and gathers the mind;
this is also called the "constant mind," yet one does not grasp at the marks of sentient beings.
This is precisely the non-perverted mind within Prajñā;
when these four minds are in constant correspondence from moment to moment,
it is called the Great Wisdom of Expedient Means (mahopāya-jñāna).
Thus, one is able to realize the essence and give rise to its function.
However, these various manifestations of sovereign activity are as they appear to ordinary beings.
This is called conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
because it involves conceptual differentiation;
it is that which is perceived within the minds of the sages.
It is precisely the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
because it is free from conceptual discrimination (nirvikalpa).
Therefore, it is said:
What are called the two truths are in reality one.
It is like a drunken person.
Through deluded vision, one perceives the house as spinning;
that is, one speaks of a spinning house and a non-spinning house.
In reality, it is the house seen spinning by the intoxicated person.
This is precisely the house that the awakened person sees as unchanging;
there are not two houses.
Second, a detailed explanation of the differences in perceptions according to individual capacity.
First, the two bodies are distinguished based on their supporting consciousnesses;
second, they are distinguished based on what is perceived by the faculties of sentient beings.
This is the first [section].
However, because it accords with the various perceptions, hearings, and so forth of sentient beings,
there are diverse and differing modes of activity.
This activity is of two kinds.
First, based on the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna*):
that which is perceived by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body).
This person does not know that it is the reflected images of the evolving consciousnesses that appear;
they see them as coming from the outside and grasp at the boundaries of forms.
However, the Buddha’s transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) are without limit. One might ask:
"If the Tathāgata has no objective realm or activity within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), [how can there be such manifestations?]"
How is it that sentient beings perceive the Buddha as having various differences,
even down to his coming and going, sitting and reclining,
and manifesting such matters as birth and nirvana?
Is it not the conventional truth?
Therefore, the present commentary states:
it merely accords with the seeing, hearing, and so forth of sentient beings.
Regarding the manifestation of the reflections of the evolving consciousnesses: when the eight consciousnesses manifest and evolve,
within their subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga),...
The manifestation of the Buddha’s body as an image is the objective part (*nimittabhāga*).
This is what is perceived by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles,
and it arises from the transformation of the common-characteristic consciousness (*sāmānyalakṣaṇavijñāna*).
The reason these images appear is that they originally do not come from outside the mind;
it is only those ordinary beings and followers of the Two Vehicles who [perceive them as such].
Because they do not know that there is the *ālayavijñāna*,
they do not know that the bodies manifested by the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings can serve as the substantial basis (*bhāva*) for the sentient beings within the minds of those Buddhas.

Not knowing that the Buddha-body perceived by sentient beings within the minds of the Buddhas is itself transformed into a reflected image based upon the body manifested by those Buddhas within the minds of those sentient beings.
Therefore, it is said that seeing comes from the outside;
this refers to grasping at the boundaries of forms.
Although that [seeing] falsely calculates that it comes from the outside, [it does not].
In truth, it does not exist externally.
Although that [manifestation] falsely grasps at limits,
its essential nature as a transformation body is originally without limit.
This emanation body is the very function of True Suchness; thus,
it is simultaneously the reward body and the dharma body.
Because the function of *tathatā* cannot exist apart from the essence and characteristics of *tathatā*,
one should therefore uphold it without beholding its summit.
Maudgalyāyana could not fathom the extent of its sound;
it reached as far as the entire land and even the cast metal [statues].
All Buddha images, whether carved in wood or painted on paper.
The three bodies are all perfectly manifest,
and the four virtues are without diminution;
one must not mistakenly follow the common people who are like those born blind.
Those of the Two Vehicles are like blind people;
claiming that [this] is not the true Buddha,
they themselves fall into the midst of distorted views.
The second is based on the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*);
this refers to all bodhisattvas from their initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*) up to the ultimate stage of a bodhisattva (*bodhisattvabhūmi*).
That which is seen by the mind is called the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya).
This body possesses immeasurable forms.
Form possesses immeasurable marks;
these marks possess immeasurable secondary characteristics;
this is the fruit that serves as the support for their abiding.
It is also adorned with immeasurable merits,
appearing in infinite and boundless ways according to what should be seen.
It is boundless and uninterrupted.
It is not seen in this way outside of the mind; rather, that very body of the Buddha perceived by the bodhisattva must also necessarily be seen by means of visual consciousness.
The manovijñāna observes that there is only the ālayavijñāna,
which takes the entirety of tathatā as its essence.
This is neither identical to nor different from the Tathāgata. Therefore,
according to what is perceived,
one should know that this is based upon the body of a Buddha within one's own mind as its substantial essence.
One returns to the transformations of reflections within one's own mind as the objects of cognition;
the primary essence does not exist outside the nature of my mind,
and the reflected image does not exist outside the cognizing mind.
Therefore, it is called the "consciousness that relies on karma.
The initial arousal of the mind refers to the first stage of the initial arousal of the mind in the Sudden Teaching.
Because they have partially realized *tathatā*,
they are able to see the Buddha’s enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*). This enjoyment body...
Because they accord with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there are immeasurable forms; for each and every form,
[there are immeasurable colors].
Furthermore, because it accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there are immeasurable marks;
according to each individual mark...
Furthermore, because it accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
there are immeasurable marks of excellence;
these are the fruits of the support upon which one dwells.
This is precisely the Land of True Reward Free from Obstructions;
it is also so called because it accords with the Dharma-nature.
For this reason, it is adorned with immeasurable merits.
However, this too relies upon the Buddha’s own enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) and its land as the substantial basis (*bimba*),
which he himself transforms into an appearance to serve as the direct object of cognition (*ālambana*).
For this reason, it is called the "other-enjoyment body" (*parasambhogakāya*) and its land.
Therefore, according to the respective capacity of each bodhisattva’s mind,
those on the first stage see a hundred worlds,
those on the second stage see a thousand worlds, and so forth.
They are of various different kinds;
it is only upon reaching the ultimate stage of a bodhisattva that one perceives them as completely exhausted.
These are both termed the bodies and lands of enjoyment for others.
For example, it is like the light of a lamp:
although each ray of light interpenetrates the others, [they remain distinct].
They mutually act as the illuminator and mutually act as the illuminated,
in infinite, overlapping layers.
This is because each remains unmixed with the others.
Reflect on this, reflect on it!
Do not say that there is a substance and a shadow.
This would then not be the complete aspect of *vijñapti-mātra*,
nor would it be the *dharmadhātu* of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*).
Question:
Question: What is it like for a bodhisattva prior to the Stage of Rejoicing (pramuditā-bhūmi) to perceive? Answer:
If it is within the gradual teaching,
it is the same as what is perceived by ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles;
if it is within the sudden teaching, [it is otherwise].
One is able to see [these qualities] identically to what was seen at the initial stage of abiding;
however, one has not yet attained the capacity for spontaneous and constant vision.
These are the various merits.
It is because it is accomplished through the perfuming of untainted practices such as the *pāramitās*,
as well as through inconceivable perfuming;
for it possesses the characteristics of boundless merit, joy, and bliss.
It is also called the *saṃbhogakāya*. Although every single merit is inherently complete by nature,
one must nevertheless cultivate practice in accordance with that nature.
Only when the cultivation of virtue is perfected does one attain accomplishment; yet,
although it is called "accomplishment," [it is merely a designation].
Furthermore, nothing is added to these innate virtues;
they are called "fruits of retribution" only in relation to the causes cultivated through practice.
Within the Buddha's portion,
the self-enjoyment reward body (sambhogakāya) is itself united with the dharma body (dharmakāya).
It is non-dual and without distinction.
The bodhisattva relies upon it as the fundamental objective realm,
which manifests as a reflected image that is perceived.
This is precisely what is called the *parasaṃbhoga-kāya* (the body of enjoyment for others).
First, the classification of the two bodies based on the supporting consciousnesses is concluded.

Second, the classification of their coarseness and subtlety based on what is perceived by the capacities [of sentient beings]—specifically, that which is perceived by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and others—is as follows:
This is its coarse function,
which manifests in various distinctions according to the differences among the six realms of existence.
That which lacks the characteristics of infinite merit and bliss is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
This refers to a bodhisattva at the initial stage of practice.
One perceives the activity of the middle grade;
through profound faith in *tathatā*,
one attains a partial vision.
One knows that the body of the Tathāgata neither goes nor comes,
and is without interruption.
These are manifestations of the mind alone,
not separate from suchness;
yet this bodhisattva...
They are still unable to abandon subtle conceptualization because they have not yet entered the stage of the Dharma-body;
such is the case for the Bodhisattva of Pure Mind.
One perceives its subtle functions;
thus it becomes increasingly superior,
even unto the ultimate stage of a bodhisattva.
Seeing them to their ultimate end—
this is the subtle function;
it is the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya).
Because there is the karmic consciousness,
one perceives the Enjoyment Body; if one were separated from the karmic consciousness, [one would not perceive it].
Then nothing can be seen;
all Tathāgatas are, in their entirety, the Dharma-body.
Because there is no distinction between self and other, as their forms are mutually visible;
"ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth includes the two vehicles (*yāna*) as well as the external ordinary beings of the gradual teaching.
For a bodhisattva who has newly begun their practice,
there is both the gradual teaching for those within the stage of ordinary persons and the sudden teaching for those both within and beyond the stage of ordinary persons.
The Bodhisattva of the Pure Mind refers to the first stage of the Initial Resolve in the Sudden Teaching,
and the first stage, the Ground of Joy, in the Gradual Teaching.
The coarse function is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body);
it is the inferior *saṃbhogakāya*.
The medium function is...
It is accompanied by the inferior and superior *nirmāṇakāya*s;
it is also called the *saṃbhogakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya*.
As for its subtle function:
The enjoyment body of other-reception is also [such];
all are reflections manifested by the dharma-body and enjoyment-body,
not separate from the dharma-body and enjoyment-body.
How could there be any coarseness or subtlety in the Buddha?
Coarseness and subtlety reside entirely within the capacities of sentient beings.
Furthermore, as for those who employ the coarse [teachings]:
The Mahayana *śamatha-vipaśyanā* is called the pure *parikalpita-svabhāva*.
Its subtle functions within the middle [state] are all called the pure *paratantra-svabhāva*.
If one is free from the karmic consciousness,
one realizes the pure and true nature; therefore,
each and every [aspect] pervades the entire dharma-realm.
It is without admixture and unobstructed;
furthermore, no distinct color-forms of "this" or "that" can be apprehended. This concludes the second section:
the extensive explanation of the differences in perception according to individual capacities.
Question: If the Buddha’s Dharmakāya possesses no various differentiated forms or characteristics, how can it manifest the wondrous functions of True Suchness?
How is it that various forms can be manifested?
Answer: Because the Dharma-body is the substantial reality of form.
Therefore, it is able to manifest various forms;
that is to say, from the very beginning,
form and mind have been non-dual.
Because the intrinsic nature of form is itself the self-nature of mind,
it is called the wisdom-body (jñānakāya).
Because the fundamental nature of the mind is itself the self-nature of form,
it is called the Dharmakāya.
Based upon the dharma-body,
the form-bodies manifested by all Tathāgatas pervade all places.
Without interruption,
the bodhisattvas of the ten directions act according to their respective capacities.
According to their aspirations and inclinations,
they behold immeasurable bodies of enjoyment and immeasurable adorned lands.
Each is distinct, they do not obstruct one another,
and there is no interruption.
This manifested form-body cannot be conceived by the mind, intellect, or consciousness of any sentient being,
because it is the profound functioning of the sovereignty of suchness. The dharma-body is itself suchness.
Suchness is the substantial reality of all phenomena;
therefore, it is the substantial reality of form.
Since it is the substantial reality of form, [it is not distinct from form].
How difficult would it be to manifest various forms?
All the more so, since from the very beginning,
form and mind have been non-dual.
It is not that one must wait until attaining Buddhahood for there to be non-duality; rather,
it means that form is itself suchness.
Therefore, it is neither form nor mind;
yet it is also capable of being both form and mind.
Mind is precisely suchness (tathatā).
Therefore, it is neither mind nor form;
yet it is precisely that which can be both mind and form. Thus, form is itself mind.
This may then be called the body of wisdom (jñānakāya).
Thus, all things are mind-only;
the mind itself is form.
This may then be called the Dharmakāya.
Thus, all things are merely form;
yet they depend upon this Dharmakāya—which is neither form nor mind—to manifest as both form and mind.
Therefore, the form-body manifested by the Tathāgata,
which extends horizontally and exhausts the vertical [dimensions],
is called the "self-enjoyment fruition."
Bodhisattvas take this as their essential object;
each perceives it differently,
which is termed the "recompense for others' enjoyment."
Although they mutually pervade one another,
they do not occupy any specific location;
therefore, they do not obstruct one another.
There is no interruption.
As for the statement "according to what one is capable of," this refers to seeing a hundred [worlds] in the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the statement "on the second stage one sees a thousand, etc.,
according to one's wishes and inclinations," this refers to what is called exercising power through the force of one's vows.
Furthermore, it exceeds this by a hundredfold, a thousandfold,
and even up to a hundred-thousand-billion-nayuta-fold,
such that it cannot be calculated or known.
These manifested form-bodies are all the profound and wondrous functioning of the sovereign power of True Suchness (tathatā);
although they are fundamentally not separate from the nature of the mind, consciousness, and awareness of sentient beings.
Because they do not awaken due to ignorance,
their deluded thoughts entangle themselves;
therefore, they are unable to engage in contemplation.
The two individual explanations of the two gates are completed.
Third, the conclusion indicating that they are not separate from the two.
First, the formal presentation of the gate of contemplation.
The two metaphors illustrate non-duality.
This section has two parts;
the first indicates the intended meaning.
Second, the explanation of contemplation.
Now, for the first [part]:
Furthermore, it is in order to cause sentient beings to emerge from the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind.
Because they enter the gate of True Suchness (tathatā), sentient beings, from time immemorial,
have failed to awaken;
thus, the entire substance of True Suchness manifests as arising and ceasing.
If one abandons the mind of arising and ceasing,
where else could there be True Suchness (tathatā) to be contemplated?
Therefore, one must immediately proceed from the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind.
By contemplating that their arising and ceasing are fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing,
one is able to enter the gateway of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Second, it clarifies contemplation by showing that form and so forth are all unestablished.
"What is non-attainment? This is a general enumeration of form (*rūpa*) and so forth as the objects of observation.
"And so forth" includes the remaining four aggregates (*skandha*) as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
That is to say, one analyzes gross matter until it gradually reaches the level of atoms,
and further divides these by their spatial dimensions.
By analyzing these atoms,
one sees that all forms, whether gross or subtle,
are merely images discriminated by the deluded mind.
In reality, nothing exists; this first demonstrates that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is not established.
Even if atoms were to possess spatial dimensions, they could then be further analyzed.
It is certainly not substantially existent.
If it lacks spatial parts,
it would then not be matter (rūpa).
Therefore, one should know that all coarse and subtle forms are merely the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) manifested by the deluded mind;
outside the mind, there are no real forms whatsoever.
Question:
The analysis of form (*rūpa*) is a contemplation of the Hīnayāna.
How is it employed in the Mahāyāna?
Answer: The Hīnayāna analyzes form and merely reveals the emptiness of the person.
In the Mahāyāna, form is analyzed to reveal that the dharmas of manifest color are fundamentally empty; therefore,
it is said that dharmas have no distinction of "great" or "small."
Whether one succeeds on a large or small scale depends on the person.
The parable of the ointment that prevents chapped hands is worthy of deep reflection.
Investigating the remaining aggregates,
one gradually arrives at the moment;
one investigates this very moment.
The distinctions between their characteristics are not uniform; next, one contemplates that the four aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are unestablished.
One investigates the mental phenomena of a single moment through the four phases of activity, namely: the unarisen.
Desire arises; having arisen, it gives rise [to birth].
Once born, [it persists].
There is no abiding for even a moment;
there is not the slightest real dharma, but only names and designations.
The unconditioned dharma is likewise thus;
it is apart from the dharma-realm.
Ultimately, it cannot be obtained; next, one contemplates that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are not established.
The arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of form and mind in every moment are called conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Regarding this conditioned,
one provisionally designates the name "unconditioned";
yet even the conditioned cannot be apprehended.
Non-existence (*abhāva*) is subsumed within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) among the eighteen elements;
it is merely an objective image perceived by the sixth consciousness.
How could it exist apart from matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*)?
Is there a real, eternal dharma called the unconditioned?
Know that it is thus for all dharmas throughout the ten directions.
Since both the conditioned and the unconditioned are not established, [they do not exist].
Then, within the worlds of the ten directions,
what further dharma could there be to achieve? This, then,
is birth-and-extinction without intrinsic nature.
It is clear that the very essence [of this] is True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This concludes the first section, which correctly demonstrates the gate of contemplation.
Second, the metaphor illustrating non-duality is like a person who has lost their way.
This means taking east for west;
while the directions themselves do not actually shift,
sentient beings are likewise [mistaken].
Due to the delusion of ignorance,
one says that the mind moves,
yet in reality it does not move.
If one knows that the moving mind is itself neither arising nor ceasing,
one immediately enters the gate of True Suchness (tathatā). This very mind, manifesting in this moment,
is in its nature True Suchness.
Sentient beings falsely perceive arising and ceasing within True Suchness (tathatā),
just as a person who has lost their way mistakes the east for the west;
yet, apart from True Suchness, there is no arising or ceasing.
Although a deluded person may claim that east is west,
east remains east; thus,
what the deluded person calls "west" [is actually east].
The original source is precisely the awakening of the person to the East;
this can be likened to the fact that outside of arising and ceasing, there is no such thing as True Suchness (tathatā).
It is said that the mind is movement.
To take the east as the west is to mistake the True Suchness for birth-and-death;
yet the mind is in reality unmoving.
Combining this with what preceded it, the East remains truly the East.
This is because apart from arising and ceasing, there is no such thing as True Suchness (Tathatā).
Therefore, if one can know that the moving mind is itself non-arising and non-ceasing, [one realizes the truth].
For example, that which is known as "west" is fundamentally "east";
this is precisely entering the gate of True Suchness (tathatā).
The single mind is divided into the two gates of delusion and awakening;
yet these two gates ultimately consist of nothing other than this single mind.
It is simply a matter of valuing the knowledge that overturns that delusion.
"Delusion" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). "That which is called" refers to...
This is precisely deluded thought.
That which knows it is precisely initial enlightenment.
One should understand it in this way; there is no other knowledge.
Therefore, it is said that initial awakening (shijue) is identical to original awakening (benjue).
The initial exposition of the true meaning is hereby concluded.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu of Lingfeng.
Part Two: Counteracting Erroneous Attachments. First, a general presentation of the two views; second, a detailed explanation of the two views.
Now, the first.
Regarding the counteraction of false attachments:
all false attachments arise without exception based upon the view of a self.
If one is free from the view of self,
there will be no false attachments.
There are two kinds of the view of self.
There are two kinds of self-view:
