Furthermore, afflictions are distinguished as being either within or outside the realms;
for each individual root of goodness,
there is a corresponding relationship with each respective affliction.
Each of these should be analyzed through four propositions:
for instance, there may be an abundance of wholesome roots and a paucity of afflictions.
Either their roots of goodness are abundant while their afflictions are thick,
or their roots of goodness are meager.
Afflictions are thin,
or roots of goodness are few;
afflictions are thick.
With their myriad distinctions and thousandfold differences,
they cannot be treated as a single category;
all are subsumed within the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi).
Some encounter Buddhas and various bodhisattvas,
making offerings to and serving them,
while practicing all manner of spiritual disciplines.
Before ten thousand great kalpas have been fully completed,
one may encounter conditions in the interim that cause the mind to be aroused.
What kind of conditions are these?
That is to say: either beholding the physical form of the Buddha,
or making offerings to the Sangha,
or being instructed by those of the two vehicles.
Or one may see others resolve their minds;
these various resolutions of mind are all as yet undetermined.
If one encounters adverse conditions and at times regresses to the stages of the two vehicles, one meets Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and practices all the various deeds.
It may be said that there are causes and conditions;
it is simply because ten thousand great kalpas have not yet been fulfilled and the ten minds have not yet reached perfection.
Therefore, although they may give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment upon encountering conditions,
they are not yet able to enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Even if ten thousand kalpas were to elapse, [they would still not do so].
Thus, upon seeing such conditions as making offerings to the Sangha and so forth,
one may resolve to enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Do not say that these conditions are not favorable ones.
However, because the power of their accumulated causes is weak,
they differ from the two types of resolve— great compassion and the protection of the Dharma; therefore, even when encountering favorable conditions, [they do not attain it].
Thus one is able to give rise to the bodhicitta;
yet, even if one encounters adverse conditions,
there is the possibility of regressing and falling into the stages of the two vehicles.
The first explanation, the accomplishment of faith, is concluded.
Second, the explanation of the arousal of the mind has three parts.
First, the explanation of the mind that is aroused.
Second, the explanation of the practice of generating the mind of enlightenment;
third, the explanation of the benefits of generating the mind of enlightenment.
Regarding the first of these, there are two parts.
First, the formal explanation;
second, the resolution of doubts.
Now, the first.
Furthermore, there are briefly three types of the resolve for enlightenment arising from the perfection of faith:
first, the generation of an upright mind.
First, by means of correct mindfulness in accordance with reality, one contemplates the dharma of suchness.
Second, by generating a profound and earnest resolve,
one delights in accumulating all virtuous practices.
Third, one should give rise to the mind of great compassion, vowing to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings. True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the foundation of all practices;
yet, one should not fail to cultivate various virtues while remaining mindful of True Suchness.
Wholesome [roots] have no means by which to accumulate.
Even if there are various kinds of wholesome deeds,
they all become tainted and conditioned.
If one does not contemplate True Suchness (tathatā), one cannot uproot the manifold sufferings; for suffering cannot be uprooted [without that contemplation],
even if one were to direct one's thoughts toward sentient beings.
This merely serves to give rise to craving and views;
therefore, one must first develop a straightforward mind.
True Suchness is inherently endowed with boundless merit.
The principle must be clearly elucidated;
therefore, in accordance with True Suchness,
one gives rise to a mind of profound respect.
Suchness is precisely the mind-nature of sentient beings.
Out of compassion for those who are deluded regarding this, one accords with Suchness.
It is the arousal of the mind of great compassion.
The upright mind is the arousal of the mind that accords with the principle of the true cause.
The virtue of the Dharma-body is accomplished;
from this state of profound and heavy resolve,
the wisdom-mind that acts as the cause of realization arises.
The perfection of the virtue of prajñā and the mind of great compassion arise from the development of the causal condition of a virtuous mind.
Accomplishing the virtue of liberation,
the three minds are fully developed without being either excessive or deficient.
They are neither identical nor distinct;
they are inconceivable. Therefore it is said:
At the very moment of first generating the resolve for enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening;
such is the body of wisdom.
Not awakened through another,
the pure and wondrous Dharma-body is profoundly still and responds to all things.
Second, resolving doubts:
all sentient beings and all phenomena.
All are of one single dharma-realm;
there are no two distinct characteristics.
According to principle, one should simply maintain right mindfulness of true suchness (tathatā).
Why, then, must one further cultivate all virtuous deeds and save all sentient beings? Answer:
Not so. It is like a mani jewel, which is by its very nature luminous and pure.
Amidst the filth of the ore,
suppose there were a person who applied themselves with diligent mindfulness.
Yet they do not employ skillful means nor exert effort,
while desiring to attain purity.
Ultimately it cannot be obtained;
the dharma of true suchness is likewise so.
Although its essence is luminous and pure,
and it is fully endowed with all virtues,
it is nevertheless defiled by boundless adventitious dust.
Suppose there is a person who applies diligent mindfulness,
yet does not employ skillful means.
If one does not cultivate various practices while seeking purity,
there is ultimately no possibility of attainment.
Therefore, one must certainly gather all wholesome practices,
rescue all sentient beings,
and become free from those boundless adventitious defilements.
To manifest the true Dharma, first an analogy is presented,
followed by its application to the Dharma;
the text is easy to understand throughout.
The first section, explaining the mind that has been generated, is concluded.
Second, explaining the practice of generating the mind:
those skillful means of practice.
Briefly, there are four kinds: first,
the fundamental application of skillful means,
which refers to contemplating all phenomena.
Its fundamental nature is non-arising;
it is free from deluded views and does not abide in birth and death.
Furthermore, one contemplates that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions,
and that the fruits of karma are never lost.
Arousing great compassion,
they cultivate all manner of wholesome deeds to gather and transform sentient beings.
One does not abide in nirvāṇa,
because true suchness is free from the characteristics of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
This practice accords with true suchness and takes it as its fundamental basis.
This is called the fundamental expedient of practice; it takes the upright mind that has been aroused as the expedient for practice.
Not abiding in birth-and-death is the contemplation of śamatha.
Not abiding in nirvana is the contemplation of vipaśyanā;
this is cultivated within a single mind that unifies śamatha and vipaśyanā.
This accords with the dharma-nature of true thusness;
therefore, it is called the fundamental skillful means of practice.
Second is the skillful means of cessation.
That which is called shame, remorse,
and the confession of transgressions can cause all unwholesome dharmas to cease and prevent them from increasing.
Because True Suchness is fundamentally free from all characteristics of fault,
one accords with True Suchness and brings all evils to rest.
This is called the skillful means for cessation.
Third is the skillful means for increasing the roots of goodness,
which refers to [practicing] toward the Three Jewels.
Give rise to a heart of love and reverence;
honor and make offerings to them,
prostrate before them, and offer praise.
Rejoicing and entreating [the Buddhas],
one's right faith increases,
until one aspires to seek unsurpassed bodhi.
Protected by the majestic power of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha,
their karmic obstructions will be purified,
and their roots of goodness will never regress.
Because True Suchness is fundamentally free from all obscurations and endowed with all meritorious qualities,
one accords with True Suchness.

To practice virtuous deeds is called the skillful means for cultivating and growing the roots of goodness; these two are practiced by taking the profound and respectful mind that has been aroused as the skillful means.
If one wishes to increase the roots of goodness,
one must first cease evil; therefore,
regarding this single profound and earnest mind:
These two types of skillful means are both categorized as such because they accord with the nature of *tathatā* (suchness);
the text is clear on this point.
The four great vows are the skillful means of impartiality;
that is to say, one makes a vow to continue until the end of the future.
They impartially rescue and protect all sentient beings,
causing them to dwell securely in *nirvāṇa* without remainder,
by virtue of their knowledge of all phenomena.
Because their intrinsic nature is non-dual;
because they are equal to one another;
and because they are ultimately quiescent.
In accordance with these three aspects of suchness, one generates the great vow;
this is called the skillful means of the equality of the great vow. This constitutes the practice of skillful means by means of the great compassionate mind that has been generated.
Regarding "nirvana without remainder":
in the Lesser Vehicle, this refers to the extinguishing of the physical body and the cessation of cognition;
here, it refers to the eternal extinction of the two types of death.
Knowing that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-dual,
one does not give rise to notions of superior, middling, or inferior regarding sentient beings;
knowing that all phenomena are equal in their mutual relationship.
Thus, one does not give rise to notions of enmity or intimacy toward sentient beings.
Knowing that all phenomena are ultimately quiescent,
one does not give rise to the notion of employing minor means to transform them.
All of these also accord with the nature of *tathatā*.
These four skillful means are all practices undertaken in accordance with that nature.
The complete cultivation reveals the nature;
prior to the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment,
one attains its arousal through these skillful means.
Once the mind has been awakened,
one ascends to the ultimate fruit by means of these skillful methods;
therefore, it is called the direct cause for all Tathāgatas to attain the Way.
The second [section], the explanation of the practice of generating the mind of awakening, is concluded.
Third, the explanation of the benefits of generating the mind of awakening has three parts.
First, clarifying the capacity by way of reality.
Second, distinguishing faults by means of the provisional;
third, subverting the provisional by means of the real.
Now, the first [section].
When a bodhisattva arouses the mind in this way,
they obtain a partial vision of the Buddha’s dharmakāya and are able to act according to the power of their vows.

Eight manifestations appear: namely, first, descending from the Tuṣita heaven; second, entering the womb; third, dwelling in the womb; fourth, emerging from the womb; fifth, leaving home; sixth, attaining Buddhahood; seventh, turning the wheel of Dharma; eighth, entering parinirvāṇa. These correspond to the meaning in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* that "at the very moment of the initial aspiration for enlightenment, one becomes a perfectly awakened Buddha."
By partially dispelling ignorance and partially realizing *tathatā*,
it is said that one sees a small portion of the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*.
Having already seen the Dharma-body,
one is able to manifest the path through the eight phases of enlightenment;
that is to say, the pure and wondrous Dharma-body.
It is profoundly serene, responding to all things.
The eight phases of manifestation differ in their opening and closing, appearing and disappearing;
these are all according to what is perceived by sentient beings in accordance with their capacities.
One need not rely on this alone to judge the provisional or ultimate nature of the Buddha,
for the Dharmakāya realized by him cannot be conceived in terms of provisional or ultimate categories, nor can it be quantified.
Second, regarding the provisional [teaching], this eliminates faults;
yet it still cannot be called the Dharmakāya, because the contaminated karma from immeasurable past eons has not yet been eliminated.
Or, due to evil karma,
they may experience slight suffering,
yet they are sustained by the power of their vows.
It is not long before they are bound; this refers to the initial stage of the "Abiding in the Arising of the Mind" as explained in the gradual teaching,
wherein one merely severs the afflictions of views within the realm of desire,
becoming equal to the first fruit of the Lesser Vehicle.
For this reason, there may still be some slight suffering.
Nevertheless, upon attaining the first fruit, one establishes a boundary for the ocean of birth and death;
at the very slowest, one will not undergo more than seven births.
They have forever emerged from the wheel of suffering;
how much more so for a bodhisattva who has resolved their mind and is sustained by the power of the vow for enlightenment.
How could one be bound by karma for long?
Question:
Upon examining the text, there are the two characters "rán" (yet) and "yóu" (still).
This refers specifically to the person who attains enlightenment through the eight phases.
How can it be explained separately as a teaching of gradualism? Answer:
The names for the arousal of the mind are the same,
yet the provisional and the real are vastly different. The preceding section elucidated the eight phases [of a Buddha's life].
This refers to those who have entered the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Here, however,
it clarifies "subtle suffering," which refers to those who may at times fall back into the stages of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
In a certain sutra it is said that there may be bodhisattvas who have attained the mind through the perfection of faith,
yet still fall back into the evil destinies.
This is said for those who are beginners, whose minds are largely indolent and who have not yet entered the state of correctness.
This causes their vigor to increase;
it is not a statement of ultimate reality. This clarifies that even within the gradual teaching, those who have first resolved to attain awakening have already severed the delusions of views.
This is equivalent to the first fruit [of the path],
and there is likewise no possibility of falling back into the evil destinies;
however, this is merely a provisional teaching intended to encourage beginners.
Alternatively, it is possible that one might regress and fall into the stages of the two vehicles.
Question:
In a certain sutra it is said that Śāriputra had already realized the state of mind of the sixth stage in a former life,
due to the incident of a brahmin begging for his eyes.
Having fallen away from the Great Mind,
they continue to transmigrate through the five destinies;
how can this be reconciled?
Answer: Furthermore, there is a sutra that says:
"The great disciples, such as Śāriputra and others..."
All of them are Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) at the profound stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*),
who manifest as śrāvakas to lead sentient beings to conversion.
Thus, demonstrating their falling [into error] is intended as an admonition for beginners;
how could there be any cause for doubt?
This concludes the second section: the refutation of faults by means of the provisional.
Third, using the real to subvert the provisional: furthermore,
after this bodhisattva has first resolved their mind,
they benefit both themselves and others.
He practices various ascetic disciplines with a mind free from cowardice,
not even fearing falling into the stages of the two vehicles.
How much more so regarding the evil realms?
If one hears that for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
they diligently practiced various difficult and painful asceticisms.
Only then does one attain Buddhahood;
being neither startled nor terrified,
how much less would one give rise to the mind of the two vehicles?
And as for falling into the evil destinies,
through the resolute conviction that all phenomena have been so from the very beginning.

"Because of the nature of nirvāṇa": this correctly clarifies that those who first resolve their minds according to the Sudden Teaching have already entered the stage of the rightly fixed assembly (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and will ultimately never regress.
Indeed, it is not only those in the initial stage of generating the mind of enlightenment who possess this superior power; rather,
anyone who attains resolute and true faith [possesses it].
One knows that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is nirvana; furthermore,
this is not like the aspiration for enlightenment according to the provisional teachings,
which may lead one to fall into the two vehicles.
First, the explanation of the resolve through the accomplishment of faith is concluded.
Second, regarding the explanation of the resolve through practice and understanding:
as for the treatise, it speaks of the perfect cultivation in accordance with the nature.
Thus, one simultaneously possesses faith, understanding, practice, and realization.
Therefore, it is said:
"Within the initial letter A..."
It thus possesses all the merits of every syllable;
even if one were to divide it into forty-two stages,
it would be like entering the ocean and discussing its depths.
Whether shallow or deep, all are the ocean.
How could there be "faith" that is devoid of understanding, practice, and realization?
How could one allow understanding, practice, and realization to be permanently situated after faith?
Specifically, because the actual stage is difficult to fathom,
it is made easy to understand by relying on provisional means;
therefore, following the stage of faith, the stages of understanding and practice (adhimukti-caryā) are distinguished.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the elucidation of the stages;
second, the elucidation of the practices.
First, regarding the generation of the mind through practice and understanding,
one should know that it is increasingly superior.
Because the first incalculable eon was about to reach its completion;
because he attained profound understanding within True Suchness (*tathatā*);
and because he cultivated all practices without attachment—this is discussed from the perspective of perfect interfusion.
It simply takes the four skillful means within the accomplishment of faith as the six perfections.
That is to say, herein, compliance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is the fundamental skillful means of practice.
In this context, being free from the characteristics of stinginess and greed,
and being free from the objects of the five desires and so forth,
constitutes the means for cessation.
In this context, the practice of generosity, ethical discipline,
and so forth constitutes the skillful means for generating roots of goodness;
herein lie the six perfections.
"One must certainly bring sentient beings to liberation;
this is precisely the skillful means of great, impartial vows.
For now, I shall briefly discuss this according to the gradual sequence.
Therefore, it is said that they become increasingly superior.
When the first incalculable eon is about to be completed,
the provisions for enlightenment are fully accomplished.
This refers to the point of entering the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
For one who has attained profound understanding within True Suchness (*tathatā*),
the two contemplations serve as the path of means (*upāyamārga*).
One attains entry into the contemplation of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way.
That all practiced deeds are without attachment means turning from phenomena toward principle.
Even to the point of turning causes toward the fruit,
one does not cling to the three realms of existence,
nor does one cling to the two vehicles.
Second, it clarifies that when this bodhisattva practices, they know that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is free from the characteristics of stinginess and greed;
this is the pure perfection of giving (dānapāramitā),
and they practice in accordance with the dānapāramitā.
Knowing that the nature of phenomena is free from the objects of the five desires and devoid of the characteristics of broken precepts is the perfection of pure ethical discipline.
They practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) in accordance with reality;
they know that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is free from suffering and affliction, and they remain detached from the characteristics of hatred and harm.
This is the pure perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*). One practices in accordance with the *kṣāntipāramitā*,
knowing that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is free from the characteristics of body and mind.
To be free from indolence is the pure perfection of vigor;
it is the practice that accords with the *vīryapāramitā*.
Knowing that the nature of phenomena is without movement or agitation is the pure perfection of dhyāna;
it is the practice of the dhyānapāramitā in accordance with reality.
To know that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is free from all delusion and darkness is the perfection of pure wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);
it is to practice in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā*. To know that the nature of phenomena is free from stinginess, greed, and so forth [is the perfection of giving].
This is understanding;
practicing in accordance with *dāna* and the other perfections is practice.
In the Sanskrit language,
*dāna* is translated here as "generosity" (*bǔshī*). *Śīla*.
This is translated as "precept" (śīla).
Kṣānti is translated as "patience" (kṣānti).
Vīrya; this translates as "diligence. Dhyāna.
This translates as "dhyāna" (meditative concentration);
it also translates as "cultivation through reflection" and "prajñā" (wisdom).
This is translated as "wisdom" (prajñā) and also as "knowledge" (jñāna).
It refers to the characteristics of practicing the six perfections.
This is as clearly explained in the "Ten Dedications" chapter of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra;
it may be the practice of partial realization,
or it may be the practice of semblance realization.
Regarding "partial truth," it refers exclusively to the ultimate;
regarding "semblance," it refers to both the provisional and the ultimate.
One should contemplate this through the two principles of perfect interfusion and sequential arrangement.
Second, the explanation of the resolve through practice and understanding is concluded.
Third, the explanation of the resolve through realization has two parts.
First, the clarification of partial realization.
Second, the explanation of the full realization.
This section has two parts.
First, the explanation of that which is realized.
Second, the clarification of the characteristics of the mind.
This section has two parts.
First, the clarification of the realization of its essence.
Second, the clarification of the arising of function. Now, first:
regarding the realization-awakening mind (bodhicitta).
From the Stage of the Pure Mind up to the Ultimate Stage of the Bodhisattva,
what realm is realized?
That which is called *tathatā* (suchness) is designated as an "object" based upon the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
However, within actual realization,
there are no objective appearances;
this bodhisattva, by means of non-conceptual wisdom, [perceives thus].
Regarding the "Pure Mind Ground" (*śuddhacittabhūmi*): in terms of provisional designation, it refers to the first stage, the Joyous Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*);

in terms of ultimate reality, it refers to the first dwelling, the Abiding in the Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*). This is because one realizes the dharmakāya of suchness that transcends verbal expression.
The "Ultimate Ground" (niṣṭhā-bhūmi) refers to the final moment of mind following the tenth ground;
it is also called the "Ground of Equal Enlightenment" (samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi).
Regarding the statement that they are called "objects" based on the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*):
the transformation of the sixth consciousness becomes the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*),
and the transformation of the seventh consciousness becomes the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).
Whatever sixth and seventh consciousnesses sentient beings possess must have an objective referent;
it is upon this that they depend.
The provisional designation of the "expresser" and the "expressed" constitutes the objective sphere;
yet, within actual realization, there is no appearance of an objective sphere,
because True Suchness (tathatā) is devoid of any characteristic that can be grasped.
Correct wisdom does not grasp at marks;
it takes the essence and marks of *tathatā* (suchness) as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
because it does not transform and take on the appearances of *tathatā* as its object-condition.
This Bodhisattva, by means of non-conceptual wisdom,
clarifies that there is a perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*).
This refers to realizing the ineffable *dharmakāya* of *tathatā*.
This clarifies the aspect of signlessness (animitta).
It perfectly accords with Dharmapāla’s *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Reflect upon this, reflect upon it!
Question: If,
according to the ultimate truth,
the stage of the first production of the thought of enlightenment (prathamacittotpāda-vihāra) is itself called the Stage of Pure Ground (śuddhabhūmi), then...
In the previously mentioned arousal of the bodhicitta,
it was stated that one merely perceives a small portion of the Buddha’s Dharmakāya;
now, however, it is stated that one realizes the ineffable Dharmakāya of True Suchness (tathatā).
The textual meanings and purports differ greatly.
How can they be reconciled? Answer:
Previously, in order to clarify both the provisional and the real,
it was stated merely that [the Buddha] "sees only a small portion.
Now, however, because the provisional realization is identical to the real, this is so.
Furthermore, with respect to the *tathatā* realized,
there is no differentiation; however,
with respect to the wisdom that realizes it, there is.
There still remains a distinction between the partial and the complete; yet,
although there are these distinctions between the partial and the complete, they are all non-conceptual wisdom.
It is like the moon of the first night and the moon of the full moon;
their radiance and appearance do not differ.
Second, to clarify the manifestation of activity: in a single thought-moment,
one can travel throughout all worlds in the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas.
Please turn the wheel of Dharma;
act solely for the benefit of sentient beings,
without seeking to hear or receive beautiful words and phrases.
Or, for the sake of sentient beings who are timid and weak,
he manifests great diligence that transcends immeasurable eons.
They swiftly attain perfect enlightenment;
or, for the sake of sentient beings who are indolent,
they pass through immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Having practiced asceticism for a long time,
he has only now attained Buddhahood;
in this way, he manifests countless skillful means.
All are for the benefit of all sentient beings;
yet in reality, the spiritual lineage, the faculties, the arousal of the mind, and the realization of the Bodhisattvas are entirely equal.
There is no dharma that can bypass this;
it is certain that all must pass through three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) to achieve perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
It is merely according to the differences among the worlds of sentient beings—
differences in what they see and hear, their faculties, desires, and dispositions—
that the various distinctions in their practices are shown; this is prior to the realization of the Dharmakāya.
Even when they descend to transform sentient beings,
it is all for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way above;
for through various skillful means of benefiting oneself and others, they act solely to realize and unite with the essence of True Suchness (Tathatā).
Once the Dharmakāya has been realized,
even if one seeks the Buddha-way above,
it is entirely for the sake of transforming sentient beings below.
This is as clarified in the current text.
Regarding those of equal spiritual lineage (*gotra*):
they are fully endowed with both the innate seeds and the seeds of perfuming through hearing.
"Those whose faculties are equal" means that there is no distinction in the excellence of their six sense bases.
"Those whose resolve is equal" means...
They equally give rise to the three minds.
"Attaining equal realization" means they equally realize True Suchness (tathatā).
Prior to the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment,
there may exist varying depths of roots of goodness and varying degrees of thickness of afflictions.
Regarding the differences in the sharpness or dullness of the faculties,
and the varying degrees of skillful means, diligence, or indolence,
once the aspiration for enlightenment has been generated:
Upon entering the nature of co-arising and the path of effortlessness,
there is absolutely no differentiation.
It is merely because the faculties, desires, and dispositions of sentient beings differ that these distinctions are manifested.
As for the phrase "three incalculable eons":
At that time, there are no real dharmas;
they are established solely based on false conceptualization.
This is as commonly transmitted in secular tradition.
A single dream of yellow millet lasts as long as more than forty years;
a thousand years on this world are likewise but a dream.
One shall not remain in the mountains for more than seven days.
Furthermore, as it says in a sutra:
"The rishi took Sudhana by the hand."
He then spent as many eons as there are atoms in the universe praising the Buddha for fifty minor eons,
yet the great assembly perceived it as being like half a day.
Thus we know that this does not refer to the years, months, days, and hours calculated by ordinary sentiments,
but speaks instead of the measure of kalpas.
This is truly because of beginningless ignorance.
Although there is no substantial reality,
one turns from delusion back toward awakening,
as if there were gradual stages of progress.
Even if Yanruo should cease his madness,
his original head remains as it was;
yet his labored breathing will surely require a long time before it becomes peaceful.
The violent winds suddenly cease and the great ocean becomes calm;
yet even the ripples must necessarily settle only after a long time.
As soon as the sun rises,
the thick mist is instantly withdrawn;
yet the dampness must also gradually dissipate before it is entirely gone.
A single dose of āgā will suddenly dispel ten thousand ailments,
yet one's vital energy must necessarily be restored gradually.
The long-traveled guest has arrived home;
his journey comes to a sudden halt,
yet household affairs remain.
Furthermore, these must necessarily be managed in successive order;
once the Sage King ascends the throne,
the great enterprise will be settled at once.
Furthermore, governance, ritual,
and music must also be unfolded in their proper sequence;
thus, within the reality of *tathatā*, which is devoid of time or kalpas, [these are nonetheless established].
Based on the gate of arising and ceasing, three incalculable eons are established;
that is, from the first stage of the initial aspiration up to the tenth stage of dedication.
This is called the first incalculable eon,
spanning from the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*),
up to the seventh, the Far-Reaching Stage (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*).
These are called the two incalculable eons;
[the eighth is] the Immovable Stage,
up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment.
These are called the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). As for the calculation of the duration of these eons,
it may be determined by taking the Buddhas whom one has served as the basis for defining their respective limits.
Alternatively, one may clarify the vastness of time by means of the analogy of celestial raiment brushing against a stone;
such matters are not uniform.
Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of practice as discussed in terms of the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*):
Some say that the afflictions are suppressed but not yet severed;
some say that the primary [afflictions] are severed while the residual habits are sustained;
others say that the afflictions are eliminated sequentially.
Some say that the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition;
all such views are *siddhāntas* (established tenets) intended to benefit beings according to their capacities.
How could one possibly adhere to them with fixed dogmatism?
Now, to say that "all are entirely equal" refers to the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* by encompassing the ocean of fruition within the cause;
this merely dispels the great arrogance and demonic view of those who claim that the three *saṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment.
One must know that throughout the ten periods of past and present,
beginning and end do not depart from the present moment of thought;
therefore, the preceding text says:
If one hears that it is only after diligently practicing various difficult and painful austerities for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas that one finally attains Buddhahood.
Without alarm or fear,
they possess definitive faith that all phenomena have been so from the very beginning.
Since it is by nature in nirvana,
how could one insist that three great aeons constitute the gradual and a single thought-moment constitutes the sudden?
Regarding the statement that the faculties, desires, and natures differ:
those things established in the past are called "faculties," and some possess sharpness.
Alternatively, for those who are dull-witted,
that which is currently desired is called desire; or, for those who are quick to rejoice, it is so named.
Alternatively, it is called "nature" (gotra) because it is the seed of the future that is either still latent or already matured.
Or perhaps it is because [the mind] is not yet matured.
First, the explanation of that which is realized is concluded.
Second, the explanation of the characteristics of the mind: within this "arising of the mind of realization" (bodhicitta),...
There are three kinds of mind.
First is the true mind,
because it is free from conceptual discrimination.
Second is the mind of skillful means,
because it spontaneously benefits others;
third is the mind of the karmic consciousness.
"Because of its subtle arising and ceasing" refers to the fundamental wisdom associated with the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
"Being without discrimination" means...
"Every thought-moment realizes the truth.
As for the "mind of skillful means," it refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) associated with the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
Spontaneous benefit for others means that in every thought-moment activity arises,
causing the first five consciousnesses to likewise become transformative function.
The "karmic consciousness-mind" is the eighth,
the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
Its "subtle arising and ceasing" refers to...
Because the seeds of ignorance have not yet been exhausted,
they are gradually extinguished through internal permeation by wisdom.
The seeds of wisdom arise,
while the seeds of delusion cease;
this is precisely what is called the characteristic of inconceivable transformation-rebirth (*pariṇāmiki-cyuti*).
Among these, the true mind is precisely the upright mind mentioned previously;
this is the mind of skillful means.
That is to say, the aforementioned two minds of profound and great compassion—
this karma-consciousness mind—
is the fundamental basis for the preceding three minds.
In the preceding section, the accomplishment of the arousal of the mind was explained solely in terms of the agent who arouses it;
therefore, all three minds are the function of the wondrous observing wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
The mental characteristics present within the presently explained clear realization (abhisamaya) encompass both the subject and the object; therefore,
they differ from those previously mentioned in terms of their expansion and contraction, as well as their detail and brevity.
The first section, clarifying partial realization, is concluded.
Second, clarifying complete realization, has two parts.
First, manifesting signs based on provisional means.
Second, resolving doubts based on the actual reality. First:
Furthermore, this bodhisattva...
Having fully perfected the two kinds of adornment— merit and wisdom—
one attains the most supreme body in all the worlds within the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
By means of the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment,
one suddenly uproots the root of ignorance and becomes endowed with the knowledge of all modes.
Spontaneously possessing inconceivable activity,
it universally transforms sentient beings throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions; it is the basis of merit and wisdom,
and is the very essence of suchness.
The two kinds of adornments are perfected; that is,
the characteristic of true suchness (tathatā),
in which both essence and characteristic are fully manifested.
When the great function manifests before one,
one is thus able to manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, it is that which is realized by wisdom.
This is the essence of True Suchness (tathatā).
Its essence pervades the Dharma-realm,
and its wisdom is perfected.
This is the characteristic of True Suchness (tathatā).
Its characteristic pervades the Dharma-realm,
and its merit is perfected.
This is precisely the functioning of True Suchness (tathatā).
Its functioning pervades the dharma-realm,
and its essence pervades the dharma-realm.
Thus, the Dharma-body pervades the Dharma-realm;
as the marks pervade the Dharma-realm,
so too does the Reward-body pervade the Dharma-realm.
Since it pervades the entire dharma-realm,
the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is omnipresent throughout the dharma-realm;
therefore, it is said:
When one person attains Buddhahood,
the entire Dharma-realm becomes the environment and the body of that single Buddha;
although there is no obstruction, [it is so].
Furthermore, they remain unmixed,
because the nature of true thusness (tathatā) is both eternally identical and eternally distinct,
being inconceivable.
Thus, when ignorance is forever exhausted and the knowledge of all modes is attained,
there is nowhere that it does not pervade.
Furthermore, it has no location whatsoever.
Now, when it is said that one attains the most supreme body in the Akaniṣṭha heaven,
what does this mean?
For the self-enjoyment bodies of all Buddhas are in profound accord with the dharma-nature; from those who have attained equal enlightenment downward, however, it is not so.
It cannot be seen by those on the stages of pure mind;
Bodhisattvas rely upon this essence of the self-enjoyment body.
Transforming into the form of the body of the Enjoyment Body for others,
one then sees [the Buddha] seated upon a lotus pedestal,
surrounded by all the Buddhas.
According to their respective capacities and according to their respective aspirations and inclinations,
they perceive each with its particular distinction.
They are entirely without interruption,
such that only upon reaching equal enlightenment can their full extent be exhausted.
Therefore, the preceding text states that "only upon seeing [it] is it fully exhausted.
If one has not yet ascended to the Ground of Pure Mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*),
then as for the Reward Buddha on the lotus pedestal:
Since it is not within their realm,
he manifested the attainment of enlightenment in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
This refers to the Buddhas upon the thousand-petaled lotuses as elucidated in the Brahmajāla Sūtra;
it is for the purpose of guiding those of sharp faculties within the realm so that they may see the Buddhas outside the realm.
As for ordinary worldlings of vast ground,
although they may possess various infinite dispositions— whether of the One Vehicle or the Three Vehicles, and whether sudden or gradual—
they have not yet attained the four dhyānas.
For one who has not yet abandoned the fetters of desire,
even the body of Akaniṣṭha is not within their range.
Therefore, he further manifested descending from Tuṣita Heaven to Jambudvīpa and sitting beneath the Bodhi tree.
He attained equal and perfect enlightenment;
this is precisely the thousand billion Śākyamunis elucidated in the Brahma Net Sūtra,
who appear for the sake of those with dull faculties within the教化 (huàjiè) realms.
Furthermore, even though they possess sharp faculties,
they have not yet abandoned the fetters of desire;
thus, these form-realm devas undergo great transformations.
The minor transformations within Jambudvīpa are all the great functioning of True Thusness (tathatā),
and they are simultaneously the essence and marks of True Thusness itself.
Therefore, in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
it is stated that the Buddha born of this very Lady Māyā already possesses the ocean of the marks of the ten bodies.

It is not that one can conceive of departing from the *nirmāṇakāya* to separately seek the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*. One should know this regarding the stage of the first production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*).
Just as you are able to manifest the eight phases [of enlightenment] in Jambudvīpa,
you must also be able to manifest the body of the Akaniṣṭha heaven;
this is now the state of ultimate perfection.
While he is able to manifest the body of Akaniṣṭha,
he must also necessarily manifest the eight phases [of enlightenment] in Jambudvīpa; however,
the former merely clarifies that his stage of generating the resolve is shallow.
For now, it is provisionally entrusted to Jambudvīpa;
now, the ultimate stage is clarified as being profound,
and it is merely provisionally entrusted to the four dhyānas.
Regarding "wisdom corresponding with a single thought-moment":
this refers to the beginningless non-awakening as the seeds of ignorance within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
Because the seeds of ignorance within the ālayavijñāna have not yet been exhausted,
it does not associate with the discernment (prajñā) among the specific mental objects;
now, however, due to the cultivation of outflow-free (anāsrava) states over vast eons, [it has changed].
When those seeds of beginningless ignorance are extinguished until they reach the state of total exhaustion,
the eighth pure consciousness suddenly becomes associated with wisdom.
It is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
Following this single moment of union,
one attains union forevermore.
Therefore it is said: "Suddenly uprooting the root of ignorance, one is endowed with the knowledge of all modes.
This is precisely the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
It differs from the previously mentioned wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*),
the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*),
and the subsequently attained wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) in that its conventional characteristics are distinct.
Because their characteristics are not destroyed,
they are spoken of as four or eight;
yet because they are real, their characteristics are not distinct.
It is solely the wisdom of suchness.
This wisdom of suchness has no phenomenon that it does not know.
There is nothing that is not seen;
therefore, it is called the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*),
and it is also called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
It is also called the Buddha-eye. Question:
Since it is said that there is nowhere it does not pervade, [how can it be so?]
If that is so, then one may also attain Buddhahood in the first, second, or third dhyānas;
why must it necessarily be in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven?
Answer: There are two meanings to this.
First, the *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that [this refers to] Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage.
First, his station is entrusted to the fourth dhyāna,
because he manifests the attainment of Buddhahood at this very stage.
Second, it is when he is about to attain Buddhahood.
The vajropama-samādhi entered must necessarily rely upon a dhyāna accompanied by equanimity (upekṣā). Second,
the two [sections] on the interpretation of the basis and the resolution of doubts.
First, the doubt regarding the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is resolved;
second, the doubt regarding effortless benefit for sentient beings is resolved.
Now, the first [is addressed].
Question:
Because space is infinite,
the worlds are infinite.
Because the world is boundless,
sentient beings are boundless;
because sentient beings are boundless...
The distinctions in mental activities are likewise infinite;
such objects of experience have no limits.
It is difficult to know and difficult to understand.
If ignorance is severed, the characteristics of the mind will forever cease to exist.
How is it that one can comprehend all aspects and accomplish the knowledge of all aspects? Answer:
All delusive objects have,
from the very beginning,
been in reality of a single nature, which is mind alone.
All sentient beings cling to delusive objects and are unable to realize the ultimate nature of all phenomena.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas,
being free from all attachment,
are able to directly perceive the true nature of all phenomena.
Yet he possesses great wisdom that clearly illuminates all distinctions between the defiled and the pure,
employing immeasurable and boundless skillful means.
According to what is appropriate for each,
they bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings;
therefore, it is only when their deluded minds are extinguished that they can comprehend all modes of existence.
"Attaining all-encompassing wisdom and directly perceiving the true nature of all phenomena" refers to the realization of the ultimate truth through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
"Clearly illuminating the distinctions between defilement and purity" refers to...
Subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) illuminates the conventional;
because it understands the conventional through the realization of the ultimate,
it is called "subsequently attained."
It is like the eye, when cleared of its cataracts,
seeing both space and forms;
there is no sequence of priority or posteriority in the resulting perception.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Second, the resolution of doubts regarding the spontaneous benefit of sentient beings:
If all Buddhas possess infinite skillful means, [how is it that they do not manifest them everywhere?]
Since [the Buddha] is able to spontaneously benefit all sentient beings throughout the ten directions,
why do sentient beings not see the Buddha constantly,
or witness his miraculous transformations?
Or he may hear the teaching of the Dharma,
and respond:
"The Tathāgata truly possesses such skillful means."
However, one must wait until the minds of sentient beings are pure before manifesting a body for them;
it is like a mirror that has impurities.
Physical forms do not appear when defilements are present; they appear once the defilements are removed.
Sentient beings are likewise.
When the mind has not yet been freed from defilement,
the Dharma-body does not manifest;
when it is freed from defilement, it manifests— the meaning of the text may also be understood thus.
Question:
If one merely removes the defilements of the mind, one directly perceives the Dharma-body;
why then is it necessary to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, visualization of the Buddha, chanting the name, and prostration?
Answer: The Buddha is one who has first realized the nature of my own mind;
keep this in mind.
Contemplate them,
praise them, and pay them ritual homage.
All of these are sublime skillful means for removing the defilements of the mind.
The third section, the "Explanatory Division," is concluded.

*Commentary on the Net-Shredder of the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*, Fascicle Six, composed by the Lingfeng Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu. Part Four:
The Section on Cultivating Faith, divided into two. First, the formal explanation of the cultivation of the mind of faith; second, further indications of its excellence.
Alternative Expedient Means.
Of the first two [sections],
the first is the inquiry.
There are two explanations. First:
what is the cultivation of the factor of faith?
This is spoken with reference to sentient beings who have not yet entered the right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
What constitutes faith? How is it cultivated?
This was previously explained in the section distinguishing the characteristics of practicing the right path.
Having clarified that one has already entered the stage of correct determination (samyaktva-niyāma) upon generating the mind of enlightenment,
although the practices cultivated within the stage of non-determination (aniyata-pakṣa) are also briefly indicated,
they have not yet been explained in detail.
Therefore, for the sake of beginners, I shall now specifically demonstrate this once more.
Part Two: The Explanation, which has two sections. First, the explanation of faith.
Second, the explanation of cultivation. First:
faith is of four kinds.
First is faith in the root,
which means delighting in mindfulness of the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness).
Second is faith that the Buddha is endowed with boundless merit and virtue.
That is to say: constantly and joyfully prostrating, revering, and making offerings;
hearing the true Dharma;
and practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
Third, one has faith that the Dharma brings great benefit,
meaning that one constantly delights in practicing the various pāramitās for the sake of dedicating [merit] toward omniscience.
The fourth is the Sangha of those who practice with right faith,

meaning they constantly make offerings to the assembly of bodhisattvas because they correctly cultivate practices for their own benefit and the benefit of others. This refers to those who have faith in the root.
Suchness is the very root of all Three Jewels;
it refers to this present, infinitesimal nature of mind,
which is free from the marks of delusion.
Perfectly equal and impartial;
this is the great essence of True Suchness (tathatā),
which is named the Jewel of Dharma.
Although one may search for it and find it utterly unobtainable,
its nature is spontaneously and divinely liberated;
it is numinous, luminous, and never obscured.
This is precisely the Greatness of the Aspect of True Suchness (tathatā-lakṣaṇa-mahattva), which is named the Buddha Jewel.
It encompasses all form and mind, as well as the environment and its inhabitants.
The empty space of the ten directions and the thousand suchnesses and hundred dharmas are all but shadows manifested within this very moment of mind.
It is inseparable from and cannot be analytically distinguished from the mind that manifests it; there is neither "is" nor "is not.
This is the Great Function of True Suchness.
This is called the Jewel of the Sangha.
Ultimately, these three Jewels in one mind are designated as the Buddha.
Therefore, one who is fully endowed with boundless merit must certainly pay homage, show respect, and make offerings to them,
and listen to the sublime Dharma they preach.
Practicing in accordance with the Dharma,
one dedicates [the merit] toward all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).
This explains the single mind and the Three Jewels.
That which is called the Dharma of Teaching;
practicing this single mind of the Triple Gem is called the Dharma of Practice.
To realize this single mind as the Three Jewels is called the Dharma of the fruit;
therefore, it possesses great benefit.
One must certainly rely on the teachings to initiate practice,
and rely on practice to realize the truth;
one should always delight in cultivating the various pāramitās.
Those who, according to their respective capacities, realize this single mind as the Triple Gem are called the Sangha of Right Practice; therefore,
[they are distinguished] from the assembly of other bodhisattvas.
One must constantly make offerings [to the Sangha],
personally cultivate the practices that benefit both oneself and others,
and thereby enter the ranks of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the statement "making offerings to the assembly of bodhisattvas," there are two intended meanings.
First, it refers to those of initial capacity who rely on provisional, gradual teachings.
He cautioned them to distance themselves from those of the Two Vehicles,
fearing that they might be defiled by attachment to dharmas and thus fall into their respective stages.
Second, regarding those of initial capacity in the Perfect and Sudden Teaching:
since they already know that those of the Two Vehicles will certainly attain Buddhahood,
they are collectively designated as bodhisattvas.
Second, the explanation of the cultivation [of the two] has two parts:
first, the general heading;
second, the detailed explanation.
First, the cultivation of the fivefold practice is able to bring about this faith.
That which is called the gate of giving,
the gate of precepts,
and the gate of patience.
The gate of diligence and the gate of cessation and contemplation; these constitute the six pāramitās.
From the very beginning, they are practices that accord with suchness.
Regarding the exposition in five gates:
once one has attained the perfection of faith,
each and every one of these will lead to the further shore.
There is no dhyāna without wisdom,
and there is no wisdom without dhyāna;
therefore, one may speak of six [perfections].
Now, for those who have not yet entered the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
if one were to divide [the path] into two separate gates of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*),
there would be no means by which they could realize the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is why they are combined into one.
One should know that the preceding four gates are auxiliary practices,
while the gate of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is the primary practice.
By practicing the primary and auxiliary methods in conjunction,
one accomplishes the two kinds of adornment— merit and wisdom—
and thereby manifests true suchness.
The second part consists of five separate explanations:
first, the explanation of the gate of giving,
up to the fifth, the explanation of the gate of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
First, how does one practice the gateway of giving?
It means that if one sees sentient beings...
When others come to beg,
one gives away one's own wealth and possessions according to one's ability.
Abandoning one's own stinginess and attachment,
one causes them to rejoice.
If one sees sentient beings...
When pressed by peril and distress,
he employs skillful means to rescue and relieve them,
so that they may be free from fear.
If there are sentient beings who come to seek the Dharma,
one should [teach] it with what one has understood oneself.
He teaches according to what is appropriate.
When practicing these three kinds of giving,
he does not do so for the sake of fame.
They do not seek gain or offerings,
nor do they crave or cling to worldly rewards;
they contemplate only the benefit and happiness of both themselves and others.
Regarding those who dedicate [their merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and give according to their capacity:
for those who have not yet entered the stage of the fixed destiny (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
it is not appropriate to demand that they practice giving until their resources are completely exhausted.
Simply by abandoning one's own stinginess and attachment to destroy evil,
and causing others to rejoice so that they may produce goodness,
this is precisely what is called the gift of material wealth.
To provide skillful means for rescue and relief is the gift of fearlessness;
it is to [teach] by means of what one has understood oneself.
To teach according to what is appropriate is itself the gift of Dharma;
it is to speak of that which one has understood.
Thus, it is certainly not a case of willfully claiming knowledge of what one does not know; rather,
speaking in accordance with what is appropriate,
one is certainly able to accord with the intent of the four *siddhāntas*.
If one preaches the Dharma inappropriately to the capacity of the audience,
then what is spoken constitutes a non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
This is not for the sake of fame or gain.
This is the severing of present outflows;
it is non-attachment to worldly retribution.
This is the severing of future outflows.
These two constitute the turning of phenomena toward principle.
Merely recollecting the benefit and happiness of oneself and others constitutes the turning of self toward others.
To dedicate toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is precisely to dedicate the cause toward the fruit;
this occurs whenever one practices each individual action.
Only when all three types of dedication are fully present can the meaning of the pāramitās be accomplished; therefore,
they are specifically demonstrated first within the gateway of giving.
One should know that all five gates are likewise without exception.
Second, regarding the gate of ethical discipline (*śīla*), how does one cultivate the gate of ethical discipline?
It refers to the lay bodhisattva.
One should abstain from killing,
stealing, and sexual misconduct.
False speech,
divisive speech,
and harsh speech.
Frivolous speech,
stinginess and greed,
and anger and envy.
Flattery, deception, and false views—
if one has left the household life,
it is for the purpose of subduing all afflictions.
One should distance oneself from clamor and bustle,
always rely upon tranquility,
and cultivate practices such as contentment and the dhūtas.
Even regarding minor transgressions,
one gives rise to great fear, feeling shame,
remorse, and self-reproach.
Upholding the prohibitions and precepts established by the Tathāgata so that no one who sees them may have cause for reproach or suspicion,
and being able to cause sentient beings to abandon evil and cultivate goodness— this is the category of precepts for householders.
The ten wholesome actions encompass everything.
By abstaining from taking life,
one practices compassion and protects sentient beings.
Not harming even the smallest flying insect;
having abandoned stealing,
one regards even a single needle or a blade of grass [as not belonging to oneself].
Not giving and not taking;
abstaining from sexual misconduct,
one remains faithful to one's own wife and concubines.
One should cultivate the thought of contentment and abstain from false speech;
thus, one's words will be truthful.
One does not deceive anyone at all.
Being free from double-tongued speech,
one conceals faults and proclaims virtues.
Not transmitting [faults] between oneself and others,
one abandons harsh speech;
thus, there will forever be no coarseness or rudeness.
One brings joy and happiness to others;
by abstaining from frivolous speech,
one's words are always meaningful.
One does not give rise to negligence;
being free from stinginess and greed,
one constantly contemplates giving with generosity.
Having no expectations and being free from anger and envy,
one does not cause harm or affliction.
Rejoicing in the prosperity of others,
and being free from flattery, deception, and false views,
one is then loyal, virtuous, and upright.
With deep faith in cause and effect,
there is no evil that they do not cease from committing,
and no good that they do not practice.
There is nothing that is not subsumed within arising;
this constitutes the Threefold Pure Precepts (Tri-śikṣā-saṃvara). This is the category of precepts for those who have left the household life.
That is to say, the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera,
the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu, and so forth,
are all subsumed within the Mahāyāna bodhisattva precepts.
If one does not guard and uphold the precepts established by the Buddha,
one is neither a layperson nor a śramaṇa.
It cannot be designated as anything;
it is neither the Hīnayāna nor the Mahāyāna.
There is nowhere to which one may return.
"Constantly relying on tranquility" means dwelling in an araṇya.
Regarding the practitioner of the dhūta of contentment and so forth:
*dhūta* is also called *duṭṭha*.
This is translated as "shaking off.
There are twelve superior practices of contentment:
first, dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage).
Second, one should always practice begging for food;
third, one should beg for food in sequential order;
fourth, one should observe the practice of eating only a single meal per day.
Fifth, to moderate the quantity of food consumed;
sixth, not to drink fruit juices, honey syrup, or similar beverages after midday;
seventh, to wear robes made of discarded rags.
Eighth, possessing only the three robes;
ninth, dwelling among tombs;
tenth, residing under a tree.
Eleventh, sitting in the open air;
twelfth, sitting only and not lying down.
These are the twelve practices.
This is called the practice that is dignified and subtle;
Mahākāśyapa, the first patriarch in the Western Land,
practiced this supreme conduct throughout his entire life.
Among the assembly of devas and humans, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"The long endurance of the True Dharma relies entirely upon this person."
This is why he shared half his seat and invited him to sit,
entrusting the Dharma-eye to transmit the mind.
Even regarding minor transgressions, he gave rise to great fear in his heart.
It is like a life-preserving float used to cross the ocean;
even if it is damaged by as much as a single speck of dust,
there remains the danger of drowning.
Therefore, one must feel shame and remorse to rectify errors and transform toward goodness.
Through shame, one comes to revere one's own spiritual nature.
It is fundamentally non-dual and indistinguishable from the Tathāgata;
how could one willingly allow negligence to lead to wrongdoing?
To feel shame is to be mindful of one's own flaws.
The Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others see everything as it truly is;
how could one conceal such things without reforming them?
Therefore, one must repent and reproach oneself.
Ceasing evil and practicing good enables sentient beings to avoid censure and reproach,
thereby causing them to abandon evil and cultivate goodness.
Therefore, one should know that the ten precepts, the full precepts (*upasampadā*),
and so forth— each and every one of them— is the threefold pure precept (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) and each and every one of them is the Mahāyāna.
Third, regarding the gate of patience: how does one cultivate the gate of patience?
